house-of-the-risin-sun: The narrator looks back on a life wrecked in a notorious house in New Orleans. The verses trace how it happened, through a hard family background and a lover given to drink and gambling, and then turn outward into a warning to others, especially a younger sibling, not to make the same mistakes. It ends with the singer resigned to going back to that house for good. Dylan sings it with raw intensity over his own guitar, in an arrangement he learned from Dave Van Ronk.
song-to-woody: A young singer far from home speaks directly to Woody Guthrie, his hero, who is now ill. He describes a world that seems weary and worn down, then thanks Guthrie and the singers who rode alongside him for the songs they left behind. The tone is humble rather than grand: he admits he cannot match them, but says he too is out on the road and trying. It is a plain, quiet performance for voice and guitar.
talkin-new-york: A young musician tells how he came east to New York in the dead of winter and tried to break into the folk scene. He rides the subway, gets turned away from a coffeehouse for sounding too rural, and ends up playing harmonica for very little pay. Along the way he jabs at the people who exploit musicians, and finally gives up on the city for now and heads off across the river. It is a talking blues, half spoken over guitar, full of deadpan jokes.
a-hard-rains-a-gonna-fall: A parent questions a beloved son about where he has been, what he saw and heard, and whom he met. Each answer pours out as a long list of images of suffering, ruin and warning, and every verse builds to the title's prophecy. In the last verse the son says what he will do next: go back into the darkness and keep telling the world what he has witnessed. Dylan delivers it alone with his guitar, steady and grave, the question-and-answer frame borrowed from an old ballad.
blowin-in-the-wind: The singer puts a series of plain questions to the listener: how long people must suffer, how long war and injustice will go on, and how long others can look away. Each of the three verses gathers more questions and never answers them directly, and the refrain only says the answer is out there, moving and hard to hold. The tone is calm and searching rather than angry, which helped it become a civil-rights anthem. Dylan sings it simply, with guitar and harmonica.
bob-dylans-dream: Riding a train, the singer falls asleep and dreams of an old room where he and his friends once sat together by a fire, talking, laughing and certain they would never grow old. As the song goes on, the dream gives way to the knowledge that those friends have scattered and the easy certainty is gone. He ends by saying he would give anything to sit in that room once more. It is a gentle, wistful song set to an old ballad melody.
dont-think-twice-its-all-right: A man leaving a relationship at daybreak speaks to the woman he is walking away from. He tells her not to wonder why, not to call after him, and not to blame herself too much, while making it clear he feels he gave more than he got back. Each verse mixes tenderness and resentment, and the refrain shrugs off the parting as if it costs him nothing. It is set to quick, rolling finger-picked guitar.
girl-from-the-north-country: The singer asks someone traveling north to carry a message to a woman he once loved who still lives there. He worries about small things: whether she is warm enough as the winter sets in, whether her hair is still long. As the verses go on, his care for her shows how much he still misses her, though he never asks for her back. The mood is hushed and tender, sung over a softly picked guitar.
masters-of-war: The singer speaks straight to the people who build and sell weapons. Verse by verse he accuses them of hiding behind desks and walls, frightening the world into war, and sending the young to die while they stay safe and grow rich. There is no chorus and no softening; his anger grows until he says no amount of money can redeem them and wishes for their death. The tune is a stark, circling traditional melody under a bare guitar.
oxford-town: The song tells of a Southern college town turning to violence because one Black man has come to enroll. In short verses the singer describes the guns, the clubs, the tear gas and the deaths, and asks how anyone could accept it. A breezy, almost jaunty guitar tune runs underneath, so the cheerful sound sharpens the irony of the grim events. It is brief and pointed, a news story set to song.
chimes-of-freedom: Two people shelter in a doorway during a night thunderstorm, and the lightning seems to them like great bells ringing out. Each verse widens the list of those the bells ring for: the refugees, the gentle, the outcasts, the mistreated, the lonely and the misunderstood, all over the world. The refrain returns them to the simple act of watching the storm. It is long, hymn-like and visionary, sung over a steady acoustic strum.
it-aint-me-babe: A man tells a woman to step away from his window and go on her way. She wants a partner who will never weaken, always protect her and give up everything for her, and he says plainly that he is not that person. The verses list what she hopes for, and the refrain turns each hope down. The tone is gentle rather than cruel, closer to honest warning than rejection, and his guitar and harmonica keep it light.
my-back-pages: The singer looks back on a time when he was sure of everything, preaching about right and wrong and seeing the world in black and white. Verse by verse he admits how proud, rigid and self-righteous he had been, and how those certainties shut him in. The refrain makes the turn: he felt old and stiff back then and feels younger now that he has let them go. It is a reflective, self-mocking song for solo guitar and voice.
ballad-of-hollis-brown: The singer tells, mostly in direct address to Hollis Brown himself, the story of a South Dakota farmer with a wife and five children and nothing to feed them. The verses pile up his troubles: a barren farm, sick animals, no work and no help coming, until, pushed past hope, he spends his last money on shotgun shells and kills his family and himself. The bleak story ends by noting that somewhere else new lives begin. It moves over a relentless, droning guitar figure.
boots-of-spanish-leather: The song is a conversation between two lovers, one of whom has sailed across the sea. She keeps offering to send him a gift from abroad, and he keeps saying he wants nothing but her safe return. Then a letter arrives saying she cannot tell when she will be back, and he understands she is gone for good, and only then does he ask for a gift, a pair of Spanish leather boots. It is quiet and restrained, carried by gentle finger-picked guitar.
only-a-pawn-in-their-game: The song tells of the murder of a civil-rights leader, shot in the back, and then looks past the gunman to the people behind him. The singer argues that a poor white man has been taught hatred by politicians, sheriffs and leaders who use it to keep power, and that he is a tool in a bigger scheme. Each verse ends by naming him as just a pawn. The tone is cool and analytical rather than mournful, set to a plain, steady guitar.
restless-farewell: The singer takes stock of his life: the money he spent, the friends and lovers he leaves behind, the quarrels he fought and the critics who misread him. Each verse ends with the decision to say goodbye and move on. In the last verse he answers the gossip and the attacks by refusing to let them change him. The mood is weary but defiant, a slow, ceremonial farewell sung over guitar and harmonica to an Irish parting tune.
the-lonesome-death-of-hattie-carroll: The song tells how William Zantzinger, a rich young man with powerful family connections, killed Hattie Carroll, a Black woman who served tables, by striking her with a cane at a hotel gathering in Baltimore. The verses set his wealth beside her life of hard work. The refrain tells listeners to hold back their tears for now, and the last verse reveals why: the court gave him only six months. Dylan sings it calmly and precisely, and the restraint makes the anger hit harder.
the-times-they-are-a-changin: The singer calls on everyone to gather round and face what is coming. Verse by verse he addresses writers and critics, senators and congressmen, and mothers and fathers, warning each not to stand in the way of change they cannot stop. The last verse declares that the order of things is about to be turned upside down. The tone is solemn and prophetic, like a hymn or a public proclamation, sung over plain guitar and harmonica.
when-the-ship-comes-in: The song imagines the day a great ship arrives and the world turns in favor of the downtrodden. Nature itself joins in, the seas and the sun greeting the change, and then the enemies of the righteous wake in disbelief and are swept away, like the army of Pharaoh in the Bible. The tone is joyful and triumphant rather than bitter. It moves with a bright, marching rhythm on guitar and harmonica, part sermon and part celebration.
with-god-on-our-side: A young man from the Midwest recalls what his schoolbooks taught him: that in every American war, from the fighting against Native Americans through the World Wars, his country had God on its side. Verse by verse he sees how easily enemies become friends and back again, and how the arrival of weapons of mass death makes the claim more frightening. He ends troubled and uncertain, hoping that God would stop the next war. It is a long, slow ballad for voice, guitar and harmonica.
gates-of-eden: The song moves through a series of strange, dreamlike scenes full of kings, soldiers, preachers, lovers and lost travelers. Each verse sets the confusion, greed and false promises of the world against a paradise where none of those things exist. In the last verse the singer's lover tells him her dreams, and he chooses not to explain them. It is solemn and hypnotic, a long solo performance for voice, guitar and harmonica.
its-all-over-now-baby-blue: The singer tells someone that the time has come to leave, and urges them to take only what they need and let the rest go. Each verse brings a new image of an old life breaking up, from the people left behind to the ground shifting underfoot. The final verse tells them to strike a light and start over. It is a farewell that is both stern and tender, closing the album on a quiet, ringing acoustic note.
its-alright-ma-im-only-bleeding: The singer surveys a darkened world and lays out what he sees: advertising that deceives, preachers and politicians who manipulate, people who conform out of fear, and a society that worships money. The verses tumble forward in long chains of rhymes, broken by short refrains in which he insists he is unharmed, merely bleeding, and simply living. It is an unrelenting monologue over hard, insistent acoustic guitar, sustained across about seven and a half minutes.
love-minus-zero-no-limit: The singer describes his lover, who speaks softly, needs no fuss and knows more than she says. Around her, people boast, argue, chase success and make empty promises, while she stays calm and untouched by it all. The song ends on a still, faintly ominous image of a wounded bird at the window. It is a quiet, admiring love song, set to a gentle band arrangement on the album's electric side.
maggies-farm: A worker announces that he will no longer labor on Maggie's farm. In each verse he describes one member of the family that runs it: a brother who underpays and fines him, a father who bullies, a mother who lectures. He sings that he tries to be himself while they want him to be like them, so he is leaving. The refrain is a flat refusal, driven home by a loud, pounding electric band.
mr-tambourine-man: Tired but unable to sleep, the singer speaks to a street musician and begs him to play a song so that he can follow. He asks to be carried away from his own mind and worries for a while, out into a night of motion, music and forgetting. The verses drift through images of dancing, wandering and escape, always returning to the request in the refrain. Dylan's own version is gentle and mostly acoustic, with harmonica.
subterranean-homesick-blues: A rush of street-level warnings is aimed at a young listener trying to get by. The verses fly past in quick bursts, with police, informers, people mixing drugs, schooling that leads only to dull work, and fads that change by the hour. Running through it all is the advice not to trust anyone who claims to lead. It is fast, funny and paranoid, delivered almost as a chant over a rough electric band.
ballad-of-a-thin-man: The song follows Mr. Jones, a respectable, educated man who walks into a room full of strange people and cannot make sense of anything. He asks questions, takes notes and appeals to his learning and connections, but every encounter leaves him more lost. The refrain mocks him for not knowing what is going on around him. The mood is menacing and sly, built on slow, heavy piano with organ.
desolation-row: The song wanders through a broken town where figures from history, literature and legend act out absurd scenes: Cinderella, Romeo, Einstein, the Phantom of the Opera and Ezra Pound and T. S. Eliot among them. Each verse adds another strange tableau of violence, fear or foolishness, with Desolation Row standing for the place where the clear-sighted end up. In the last verse the singer answers a letter by asking for no more unless it comes from there. It is long, acoustic and hypnotic.
highway-61-revisited: In five short, comic verses, the song tells of absurd events that all end up on the same American highway. God orders Abraham to sacrifice a son there, a man with a bloody nose needs a place to go, odd goods need dumping, and finally a promoter decides to stage the next world war out there. Each tale lands in the same place, making the road a stage for everything. It is a rowdy, fast band performance punctuated by a police siren whistle.
just-like-tom-thumbs-blues: A drifter narrates his own unravelling in a Mexican border town, where the authorities are crooked, the women are dangerous and every comfort turns out to cost him something. The verses move like a slow hangover, each scene seedier and more sickly than the last, until he gives up on the place and decides to go back to New York. The tone is weary and darkly funny, carried by a loose, rolling band with piano well up in the mix.
like-a-rolling-stone: The singer turns on a woman who once lived in comfort and looked down on others, and who now finds herself alone, broke and without a home. Verse after verse he lists the friends and privileges she relied on and shows how each has failed her, then lands on a chorus that taunts and challenges at once. Beneath the scorn runs a strange sense of release, as if losing everything has set her free. Rolling organ and a long, surging band arrangement drive it.
queen-jane-approximately: Addressed to a woman worn down by her family, her admirers and the obligations of her position, the song offers a quiet alternative. Each verse names another source of her exhaustion, and each closes on the same refrain inviting her to come and see the singer once she has had enough. The mood is gentler than the songs around it on the album, half sympathy and half wry teasing, set to an easy mid-tempo band groove.
tombstone-blues: A fevered collage of America in which historical figures, biblical characters and pop-culture names collide in absurd, often violent scenes. There is no story as such; the verses pile up images of war, authority and madness, while a chorus returns the singer to his own household, where everyone is struggling to get by. The effect is satirical and breathless, propelled by a racing electric blues band and Mike Bloomfield's stinging lead guitar.
4th-time-around: The singer recounts an uneasy encounter with a lover that turns on small, awkward exchanges and a sense that neither party is being straight with the other. The story unfolds coolly and with deadpan humour, and ends with him leaving and addressing someone else entirely. Its lilting waltz melody and storyline closely echo the Beatles' Norwegian Wood, which many hear as a playful reply. The arrangement is soft and spare, built on gently picked guitars.
i-want-you: A bright, simple confession of longing, set against a gallery of strange and sorrowful characters who pass through the verses. The singer moves briskly from one odd figure to the next, each a little sad or ridiculous, but every verse returns to the same direct refrain of desire. The contrast between the crowded, surreal scenery and the plainness of what he wants gives it charm. It bounces along on a cheerful, jangling band sound with bright guitar lines.
just-like-a-woman: The singer looks back on a relationship with a woman who presents herself as poised and grown-up but, in private, comes apart like a child. The verses move from the scene around her to his own exhaustion and his need to leave, and the chorus repeats his double-edged verdict on her. The tone sways between tenderness and resentment, which has made the song both loved and argued over. It is a slow, gentle ballad with acoustic guitar and harmonica.
rainy-day-women-12-35: A boisterous romp in which the singer complains that people will attack and condemn you whatever you do, at home, at work or out in the street. Each verse lists another way of being judged, and each ends on a chorus that turns the persecution into a rowdy joke with a famous double meaning. Recorded in Nashville, it sounds like a marching brass band at a party, with laughter, shouting and loose, stumbling horns.
sad-eyed-lady-of-the-lowlands: Dylan addresses a woman he holds in awe, describing her over several long verses in a cascade of surreal, devotional images that never settle into a plain portrait. Each verse builds slowly toward the same pleading refrain, in which he asks whether he should go on waiting for her. The tone is reverent and almost liturgical rather than casually romantic. The band plays softly and patiently, swelling at each chorus, and the song stretches past eleven minutes, filling the whole fourth side of the original double LP.
stuck-inside-of-mobile-with-the-memphis-: The narrator is stranded in a town where nothing makes sense, and each verse brings another odd character his way, from lawmen and would-be lovers to advisers offering strange counsel. Between these encounters comes a weary refrain that wonders if he is doomed to stay there for good while longing to be somewhere else. The mood is comic and exasperated rather than despairing. The Nashville musicians give it a loose, rolling bounce that carries it through its seven minutes.
visions-of-johanna: Set during a sleepless night, the song finds the singer in a room with one lover, Louise, while his mind keeps drifting to an absent woman, Johanna, who seems more vivid to him than anyone present. The verses wander out into the city and through a gallery of minor figures, then return each time to that haunting pull of memory. There is no resolution; the longing only deepens as the night wears on. The Nashville recording is hushed and drifting, with organ and harmonica adding to its late-hour mood.
all-along-the-watchtower: A terse parable, the song opens with two outsiders, a joker and a thief, talking about a world where the powerful take what others make and understand nothing of its worth. Their talk gives way to a wide view from a fortress lookout, where princes keep watch as two riders approach and the weather turns. It stops on the brink of something rather than its arrival, leaving a mood of dread. The original is spare and acoustic, though Dylan later adopted the hard-rock arrangement Hendrix gave it.
as-i-went-out-one-morning: This short ballad is told by a man out walking who comes upon a young woman bound in chains. She pleads to run off south with him, and he turns her down, wary of what she wants, until the figure of Tom Paine hurries up to apologize for her and take charge. It reads like an allegory about freedom and its claims, told in a cool, deadpan voice. The arrangement is spare, just bass, drums, guitar and harmonica, like most of the album.
drifters-escape: A drifter stands trial for reasons he cannot grasp, while the judge seems sympathetic yet powerless and the jury and crowd grow hostile around him. Just as the case turns against him, lightning strikes the courthouse, and in the confusion he slips away. Brief and told like a parable, it has a tense, almost biblical feel and leaves the meaning of both the crime and the escape open. It closes the first side of the original LP at a brisk three minutes.
i-dreamed-i-saw-st-augustine: Borrowing the dream framing of the old labor ballad about Joe Hill, the singer describes seeing the saint alive, moving among the crowds in sorrow and calling out to people who have lost their way. The dream then darkens as the singer realizes he was among those who put the saint to death. He wakes in fear and shame, and the song ends in grief. Its tone is quiet and confessional, set over the sparse acoustic backing of the album.
ill-be-your-baby-tonight: A lover speaks gently to his partner, urging her to set aside her worries and the outside world and simply settle in for the night together. It is short and untroubled, with a lazy, good-humored charm and one warm promise at its heart that keeps returning. After the stern parables elsewhere on John Wesley Harding, it closes the album on a note of ease. The pedal steel of Pete Drake gives it a soft country lilt that pointed ahead to Nashville Skyline.
john-wesley-harding: A narrator tells the legend of a frontier gunman in the manner of an old outlaw ballad, casting him as a protector of ordinary people rather than a villain. The song sketches his reputation in quick strokes, a man with a gun in each hand who helps the honest and slips away whenever the lawmen close in. There is no real plot or reckoning, only the myth retold. It moves at a brisk, steady clip on acoustic guitar, harmonica, bass and drums.
the-wicked-messenger: This is a dark parable about a messenger who cannot carry a message straight. Told in the voice of an ancient scripture, the song describes a man who exaggerates and distorts everything he reports, until the people he serves finally rebuke him and tell him that if he must speak, he should bring only good tidings. It is terse and ominous, with no chorus and no wasted line, and it ends abruptly. A tight, insistent bass line drives it from start to finish.
girl-from-the-north-country-with-johnny-: Two singers send a request with someone heading north: look in on a woman one of them once loved and make sure she is safe and comfortable. The song is tender and wistful rather than bitter, a memory of a love that ended long ago but still matters. Here Dylan and Johnny Cash trade and share the verses, their voices not always in step, which gives the duet a loose, warm, unpolished charm. The backing is a gentle Nashville country arrangement.
i-threw-it-all-away: A man looks back on a love he once held and admits, without excuses, that he let it go through his own carelessness and pride. The regret is plain and personal, and from it he draws a lesson for the listener: treasure love while you have it, because it may not come again. The song is short and direct, a confession turned into advice. It is sung in the smooth, mellow voice of the Nashville Skyline period, over organ and a soft country band.
lay-lady-lay: A man asks a woman to stay with him through the night, coaxing her gently rather than demanding. The song is tender and sensual, a slow seduction in which he tells her there is no reason to leave and that he wants her near until morning. Its verses circle back to the same plea, building patience instead of urgency. Dylan sings in a soft, low croon over pedal steel guitar and an unusual, clip-clopping percussion part.
nashville-skyline-rag: This track has no words at all. It is a lively country instrumental that hands the spotlight to the Nashville session musicians, who take turns soloing on guitar, banjo, piano and other instruments over a bright, bouncing rhythm. The tone is playful and relaxed, like a band enjoying itself at the end of a long day. Short and cheerful, it serves as a light breather on the album between the more personal love songs.
tell-me-that-it-isnt-true: A man has heard talk around town that the woman he loves has found someone new and is ready to leave him. He does not accuse her; instead he pleads with her to say the stories are false, his worry growing as the gossip piles up. The song stays in that anxious, hopeful moment of not yet knowing. It is a gentle, mid-tempo country ballad, sung in a smooth voice over piano, organ and a relaxed Nashville band.
to-be-alone-with-you: A man spends the day thinking about the evening, when the work is done and he can finally be alone with the woman he loves. The mood is light and affectionate, with no conflict at all, just eager anticipation and simple contentment. The song is short and bouncy, built on a jaunty piano and a loose country rhythm. A brief spoken remark from Dylan to his producer before the music starts adds a casual, studio-floor feel.
tonight-ill-be-staying-here-with-you: A man who has always been ready to leave finally decides not to. Speaking to the woman beside him, he gives up his travel plans and lets the train go without him, choosing one night of closeness over the open road. The mood is relaxed and quietly happy, with no regret in it. Sung in the mellow, warm voice of the Nashville Skyline period, it closes the album on an easy country shuffle.
day-of-the-locusts: Dylan looks back on a day spent being honored by a famous university, and he plainly would rather be anywhere else. He describes the stiff hall, the solemn faces and his own nervous discomfort, while the loud buzzing of insects outside seems to mock the ceremony. The turn comes when he gets away and drives off toward the hills with the woman he loves. Wry and self-mocking, it is a small comic portrait of fame feeling like a trap.
if-not-for-you: A plain, grateful love song in which the singer tells his partner how lost he would be without her. He pictures a life gone dull and cold, unable to find his way, then sets it against the warmth she brings. Each verse returns to the same thankful idea, so the song works almost as a simple refrain. Bright and unhurried, it opens New Morning with a light, homespun country-folk feel.
the-man-in-me: A man admits that he hides behind a tough or distant front, and that only the woman he loves has the patience to see through it. Addressed to her, the song is a warm thank-you for being understood. It is short and easygoing, with a wordless vocal hook that comes back again and again. A rolling piano and gospel-tinged backing singers give it a loose, contented swing.
all-the-tired-horses: This is barely a song at all, more a brief, hypnotic chant. A lone rider is stuck, unable to get moving, while the hours slip away. The same couple of lines are repeated over and over by a choir of women, with lush strings swelling behind them, and Dylan himself never sings. Opening Self Portrait this way felt like a puzzle or a joke to many listeners, yet it has a dreamy, drifting beauty.
copper-kettle: An old mountain dweller speaks fondly of making whiskey the traditional way, out in the hills where nobody comes to collect taxes. He treats the craft as an inheritance passed down from his elders and as a quiet act of independence from the government. The tone is slow, proud and gently defiant rather than rowdy. Dylan sings it tenderly over soft guitar and a hushed backing, one of the more admired tracks on Self Portrait.
the-boxer: Dylan takes on Paul Simon's well-known story of a poor young man who leaves home for the city, finds little work and much loneliness, and thinks about going back. The song ends on the figure of a fighter who refuses to quit despite all the punishment he has taken. Dylan sings it as a duet with himself, one track in his smooth country voice and one in his rougher older style, slightly out of step with each other. Many hear it as strange or even playful.
cant-help-falling-in-love: Dylan takes on a much-loved romantic standard and sings it as a simple confession. The speaker admits that sensible people would warn him against hurrying into love, yet he finds he cannot stop himself and gives in completely. He likens his feeling to a river that has no choice but to run to the sea. The song asks nothing of the listener except to accept that some feelings arrive whether or not they are wise.
lily-of-the-west: An old ballad told by a man looking back on his ruin. He travels to a new town, falls hard for a beautiful woman, and believes she returns his love, until he finds her with another man. In a jealous rage he attacks his rival and ends up tried and locked away. The striking turn is that, even after her betrayal has cost him his freedom, he still cannot stop loving her, and the tale closes on that helpless devotion.
billy-1: The singer speaks directly to Billy the Kid, an outlaw on the run, as the law closes in. The verses follow him through lonely towns, card games, borrowed beds and the long ride toward the border, while a lawman who was once his friend draws nearer. Each verse returns to the same address to Billy, part warning and part lament, as if the outcome is already known. The mood is unhurried and fatalistic, a portrait of a young man living on borrowed time.
knockin-on-heavens-door: A dying lawman speaks to his mother, asking her to take away the badge and the guns he no longer has any use for. He describes the light failing around him and the sense that his time is over. The song is short, just two verses, each followed by a repeated refrain in which he says he is at the threshold of heaven. Gentle backing voices and a slow, steady rhythm give it the feel of a hymn sung at a deathbed.
forever-young: A parent offers a blessing to a child, setting out hopes for the life ahead. Verse by verse the wishes pile up: that the child will be honest, brave, surrounded by love, sure of foot and strong in spirit, and will always have a song inside them. Each verse closes with the same refrain, a wish that the child keep a youthful heart however many years pass. The album holds two recordings of it, one slow and tender, the other quicker and more upbeat.
on-a-night-like-this: A man welcomes a lover home on a bitter winter night, delighted that she is back with him. He talks of shutting out the cold, building up the fire, and staying close together while the snow piles up outside. Rather than a story, the song is a single happy moment stretched out, full of easy affection and relief. The Band back him with a loose, rolling sound that feels like a party in a warm room.
wedding-song: A man pours out his devotion to his partner, telling her she rescued him and gave his life meaning. He insists his love is greater now than ever and that he has no wish to return to the turmoil of the past. The verses build in intensity, moving from gratitude to vows that reach toward forever. It closes the album as a solo performance with only acoustic guitar and harmonica, which makes the passion sound raw and personal.
buckets-of-rain: A man tells his lover about the sorrow he carries and the simple pleasures she brings him. Between wry complaints about how hard and unfair life can be, he lists small, affectionate things he likes about her, and offers to do whatever she needs. The song settles on a shrug of acceptance: life is tough, so you get on with what has to be done. It ends the album as a quiet acoustic blues, gentle and slightly teasing.
idiot-wind: A man lashes out at a former lover and at the rumours and lies that have swirled around them. The verses heap up bitter accusations, wild images and jabs at the people spreading stories, with a chorus that names her as the source of all the foolishness. In the final chorus he turns the charge on both of them, admitting his own share of the blame. The released version is the harder full-band take cut in Minneapolis, loud and full of anger.
lily-rosemary-and-the-jack-of-hearts: A western tale told across many verses, set in a small mining town. A stranger who seems to be the Jack of Hearts arrives at the cabaret, and his presence stirs up the showgirl Lily, the jealous wife Rosemary, and the powerful man who owns the town. While a robbery unfolds down the street, tensions in the room explode into a killing and a hanging. There is no chorus; the story simply rolls forward, and the mysterious stranger slips away at the end.
shelter-from-the-storm: A worn-out man looks back on the time a woman took him in when he had nowhere left to turn. The verses describe the hostile, violent world he was escaping and the calm she offered him, each closing with the memory of her welcome. As the song goes on, regret creeps in: he has lost that refuge and wishes he could return to it. The original is a solo performance; later he remade it with a loud band on Hard Rain.
simple-twist-of-fate: The song begins in the third person, following a couple who meet one evening, walk together and spend the night in a cheap hotel. When he wakes she has gone, and he searches for her along the waterfront, hoping she will come back. In the last verse the voice shifts into the first person, revealing that the story is his own. Each verse ends by blaming chance for what happened, and the tone is sad and resigned.
tangled-up-in-blue: A man retraces a love affair that keeps breaking off and starting again over many years. The verses jump between places and jobs, from a marriage that falls apart to drifting work, a chance reunion and an old book of poems that moves him. The pronouns slip between he, I and she, so the story feels like memory shifting as it is retold. By the end he is back on the road, still looking for her. The Minneapolis version opens the album.
youre-gonna-make-me-lonesome-when-you-go: A man in a new, happy romance already senses that it will not last and that he will miss her badly when she leaves. Rather than sinking into gloom, he sounds amused and tender, comparing this love favourably with a stormier one from his past and noticing the small sights of their days together. He imagines looking for her in distant places once she has gone. It is a spare acoustic recording from the New York sessions, light on its feet.
tears-of-rage: A parent speaks to a grown child who has turned away, recalling the hopes and care given in the past and the hurt of being forgotten. The verses move from memories of raising the child to a bitter sense of betrayal, while the refrain dwells on grief and the lateness of the hour. The mood is slow and mournful, closer to a hymn than a complaint. Dylan wrote the words and Richard Manuel of the Band wrote the music.
this-wheels-on-fire: The speaker tells someone that he will return, and that when he does, the debts and promises between them will have to be settled. The images are mysterious and full of menace, building toward a refrain about a burning wheel rolling down the road that threatens to burst apart. Nothing is fully explained, which makes the warning feel all the more unavoidable. Dylan wrote the words and Rick Danko of the Band wrote the music.
you-aint-goin-nowhere: A cheerful song about waiting for a loved one to arrive. The speaker mixes everyday details with odd, playful nonsense, and the refrain urges patience and comfort, as if the wait itself might be enjoyed. Its tone is relaxed and good-humoured, a song of contentment rather than longing. The Byrds released a cover of it in 1968, years before his own recording was officially issued.
black-diamond-bay: A long story song set at a hotel on a tropical island. A cast of strangers, among them a mysterious woman, a soldier, a gambler and a desperate man, each pursue their own small dramas as a volcano begins to erupt. The island and everyone on it are swallowed up. In the final verse the scene cuts to a man far away who sees the news on television, shrugs and moves on. Dylan co-wrote it with Jacques Levy.
hurricane: A long narrative that lays out the case that the boxer Rubin Carter was wrongly convicted of a triple murder. It opens on the night of the shootings and follows how police, witnesses and the courts built a case against him, presenting race and corruption as the real reasons for his conviction. The song is told with anger and urgency, ending with a plea for his freedom. Co-written with Jacques Levy, it drives forward with a prominent violin.
isis: A man marries a woman named Isis and then, restless, rides away from her. He falls in with a stranger who promises treasure, and the pair travel through cold, wild country to rob a tomb, only for his companion to die and the prize to prove empty. Changed by the ordeal, he returns to Isis, and the song ends on their reunion. It unfolds like a myth or dream. Co-written with Jacques Levy, it was a staple of the Rolling Thunder Revue shows.
joey: A long, sympathetic ballad about the New York gangster Joey Gallo. It traces his rise in the underworld, his years in prison and his return to the streets, presenting him as a man who wanted peace and was hunted by rivals. It ends with his violent death in a restaurant, and the refrain asks why he had to die that way. The tone is mournful, treating him almost as a folk hero. Dylan co-wrote it with Jacques Levy.
oh-sister: A man pleads with a woman to let him close, appealing to the faith and family bonds they share. He reminds her that they were raised under the same guiding hand and that life is short, so it would be wrong to hold back. The tone is earnest and slightly anxious, as though he fears she may refuse. Co-written with Jacques Levy, it is sung as a duet with Emmylou Harris, whose voice gives the plea added weight.
one-more-cup-of-coffee: A man prepares to leave a mysterious woman whose family seems wild and dangerous, and asks for one last drink before he sets off down into the valley. He describes her beauty and her strange household, and admits that she does not truly love him. Each verse returns to the same request, as if he is delaying the parting. The mood is dark and exotic, with Emmylou Harris singing harmony.
sara: A husband speaks to his wife, recalling scenes from their life together: the children playing, places they visited, the early days of their love. The tender memories are mixed with a growing sense that she is slipping away, and his praise of her becomes a plea for her to stay. The song alternates verses of memory with a refrain that simply calls her name. Written by Dylan alone and named for his wife, it closes the album.
changing-of-the-guards: A dense, dreamlike allegory that runs for more than six minutes and opens the album. It moves through images of a long struggle, a lost woman, merchants and thieves, and powers that seem ready to fall, without telling a straightforward story. The verses build toward the sense that an old order is ending and something new must take its place. The arrangement is big and full, with horns and backing singers driving it forward.
is-your-love-in-vain: A man who has been hurt before questions a new lover about what she really wants from him. He asks whether she needs him or just his company, whether she understands his life, and whether she could be the partner he hopes for. The questions sound cautious, even demanding, as he weighs up the risk. In the end he decides to take the chance and give his heart anyway.
senor-tales-of-yankee-power: A weary traveller speaks to a mysterious guide he calls Señor, asking where they are heading and how long the journey will last. The verses are full of uneasy questions and scenes from a harsh landscape, hinting at a past love and a world close to catastrophe. By the end his patience runs out and he longs to break free and tear things down. The tone is brooding and tense, a dark journey with no clear destination.
gonna-change-my-way-of-thinking: The speaker announces that he is going to change how he thinks and lives, setting aside old habits for a new, stricter code rooted in his faith. The verses describe the corruption around him and his resolve to stand apart from it. The tone is tough and determined rather than gentle, delivered over a hard, bluesy groove. He later recorded a reworked version as a duet with Mavis Staples for a 2003 tribute album of his gospel songs.
gotta-serve-somebody: The singer runs through a long list of people, from the powerful and famous to the ordinary and the poor, and tells each of them the same thing. Whatever their status, they will end up serving one master or another, either good or evil. The refrain hammers that choice home after every verse. The tone is steady and certain, almost preaching. It won Dylan the 1980 Grammy for Best Rock Vocal Performance, Male.
i-believe-in-you: The singer describes being shunned by friends and treated as an outsider because of his new faith. Each verse sets the rejection he faces against his determination to keep believing, whatever the cost. The tone is quiet and resolute rather than defiant, a private devotion spoken aloud. He played it on Saturday Night Live in October 1979 as one of three songs.
man-gave-names-to-all-the-animals: A playful retelling of the story of the first man naming the creatures in the garden. Each verse describes an animal he comes across, its look and its habits, and then the name he gives it, so the listener can guess along. In the final verse a snake appears, and the song stops before naming it, leaving a sly hint of trouble ahead. It was published as an illustrated picture book for children in 2010.
precious-angel: The singer speaks to the woman who brought him to faith, grateful that she opened his eyes to what he had been missing. Between those thanks he turns outward, scolding friends and others who cling to comfortable illusions and warning that a spiritual battle is under way. The mood is bright and urgent rather than solemn, a love song and a sermon at once. Mark Knopfler's lead guitar threads through the full, buoyant band sound.
slow-train: The singer looks around at his country and the wider world and does not like what he sees: greed, hollow preachers, leaders who serve themselves, and people who have traded conscience for comfort. Verse by verse the complaints pile up, some public and some personal, and each time the refrain points to something slow but unstoppable approaching. The tone is weary and stern, more warning than rage, carried by a patient, rolling groove that gives the album its name.
when-he-returns: Close to a prayer, the song has the singer reasoning with himself and with anyone listening about pride, struggle and the futility of resisting a greater power. He asks how long a person can keep fighting what they already know, then lets the argument rest in trust that a coming return will settle every question. It moves slowly and builds in intensity without ever raising the tempo. As the album's closer, it is only Dylan's voice and Barry Beckett's piano.
when-you-gonna-wake-up: The singer runs through what he sees as the hypocrisies of modern life, from false teachers and self-serving leaders to people who chase pleasure while ignoring what matters. Each verse adds new targets, and each chorus comes back to the same blunt question of when the listener will finally rouse themselves and act. It is less a lament than a confrontation, delivered with the force of a preacher pounding the pulpit over a hard-driving band.
pressing-on: The singer describes people who doubt him, try to shake him or pull him back, and answers each with the same resolve to keep moving toward a higher calling. There is no turn in the story; the song works by repetition, its determination growing as it goes. It starts quietly and swells into a full gospel performance with backing voices. Years later, in the 2007 film I'm Not There, the song is sung by John Doe.
saved: A joyful testimony, the song has the singer looking back on a life he now sees as blind and headed for ruin, and celebrating the rescue that turned it around. The verses move from that old state to gratitude, with the title returning as a shout of relief. There is no doubt or hesitation in it, only celebration. The title track is co-credited to Dylan and bassist Tim Drummond, and it moves at a quick, exuberant gospel pace.
solid-rock: The singer insists he is holding on to a foundation that cannot be moved, whatever pressure, mockery or temptation the world puts in his way. The verses sketch the forces arrayed against him and recall the suffering that, in his belief, made his rescue possible, while the chorus hammers home his refusal to let go. It is fast, insistent and almost defiant in tone. It was a driving fixture of the 1979 to 1980 gospel concerts.
every-grain-of-sand: In a quiet moment of reckoning, the singer looks back over his failings, temptations and regrets without excuses. He describes swinging between feeling watched over and feeling utterly alone, yet keeps finding signs of a guiding purpose in the smallest things around him. The song never preaches; it reads like a confession and a gentle act of acceptance. Unhurried and spacious, with harmonica, it closes the album and is often counted among his finest songs.
lenny-bruce: The singer remembers the comedian Lenny Bruce, who died in 1966, as someone who told uncomfortable truths and was punished for it. He argues that Bruce was no criminal, contrasts him with people who did real harm and went free, and recalls a brief personal encounter with him. The tone is fond and a little rueful rather than angry, a tribute from someone who admired his nerve. Dylan delivers it as a slow ballad led by piano.
shot-of-love: The singer is surrounded by trouble: enemies plotting against him, people who misjudge him, and temptations that promise relief but deliver none. He rejects one easy fix after another and keeps returning to the one thing he says can truly heal him, the love named in the title. The tone is gritty and restless rather than serene. The title track was produced by Bumps Blackwell, known for his work with Little Richard, and has a raw, rocking edge.
dont-fall-apart-on-me-tonight: Late at night, a tired and uncertain man talks to the woman beside him, admitting regrets about the life he has led and the person he might have been. He wonders aloud about what has passed and what might still come, but keeps circling back to one simple request that she stay strong with him until morning. The mood is tender, worn and a little wry. It closes the album on a quiet, intimate note.
i-and-i: The singer slips out at daybreak, leaving a woman asleep, and walks through a stark landscape while turning over questions of guilt, justice and the impossibility of facing God directly. The verses wander between small observations and heavy moral thought, and the refrain returns to the title, borrowed from a Rastafarian expression for the self joined with God. The mood is uneasy and solitary, set to a loping, reggae-tinged rhythm.
jokerman: The singer addresses a mysterious, ever-changing figure who moves freely through a crowded dreamscape of biblical scenes, false prophets and looming tyrants. Each verse piles up vivid images, and the chorus calls out to the Jokerman directly, half in admiration and half in frustration that he does nothing to stop what is coming. Whether he is a savior, a trickster or the singer himself is left open. The opening track rides a light, reggae-inflected groove.
license-to-kill: The song looks at humanity's drive to conquer, from reaching into space to waging war, and suggests that man has been taught to think of himself as master of everything. Against that sweeping indictment stands a single woman who watches and understands, and who keeps asking who will finally take away his power to destroy. The tone is grave and accusing. Dylan later played it on Late Night with David Letterman in March 1984 with the punk band the Plugz.
neighborhood-bully: Using one extended, sarcastic metaphor, the singer describes a small figure scorned as a bully for refusing to be wiped out, though outnumbered and surrounded by hostile neighbors. Verses trace a long history of exile and persecution and mock the double standard by which survival itself is condemned. The irony never breaks; the narrator keeps repeating the accusation while showing how unfair it is. The song is widely heard as a defense of the state of Israel, set to a forceful rock arrangement.
sweetheart-like-you: The singer meets a woman in a dim, unwelcoming place run by men who are absent or not to be trusted, and asks why someone like her is there at all. He offers observations about power, ambition and the roles people are pushed into, mixing admiration with something close to condescension. The tone is gentle and wry, a quiet conversation more than a story. It was the album's first single, built on a slow, easy groove.
union-sundown: The singer takes an inventory of everyday goods, from clothes to cars, and notes that almost none of it is made at home anymore. He blames corporate greed that ships work abroad to cheap labor, but also turns a skeptical eye on unions that have lost their way. The tone is sardonic and combative, with each verse adding new examples before the chorus tolls the end of an era. It plays as a hard, punchy rocker with backing singers.
dark-eyes: The singer moves through a night world where people chase money, fight and forget each other, and he feels like a stranger to all of it. Instead of joining in or condemning it, he steps back, troubled and detached, and the one thing that holds him is the steady gaze of the dark eyes in the title. The tone is hushed and haunted. The closing track is just Dylan with acoustic guitar and harmonica, a stark contrast to the rest of the album.
tight-connection-to-my-heart: The singer is caught in a relationship full of suspicion and unease, where he feels watched, misread and unsure of where he stands. The verses jump between fragments of scenes, some tense and some oddly comic, while the chorus keeps asking whether anyone has seen the love he has lost. The tone is restless and a little paranoid. He reworked it from an unreleased Infidels-era song, giving it a polished mid-eighties sound with backing singers.
when-the-night-comes-falling-from-the-sk: The singer addresses a woman who turned him away, and his hurt hardens into a warning that she will see him again when darkness finally falls. The verses mix wounded pride with images of upheaval and judgment, so a personal grudge starts to feel like something larger. The tone is brooding and insistent, building rather than resolving. At seven and a half minutes it is the longest song on the album.
brownsville-girl: The narrator recalls watching the Gregory Peck western The Gunfighter and lets the film bleed into his memories of a road trip across Texas with a woman he has since lost. The story drifts between past and present, scenes from the movie and scenes from his own life, until it is hard to tell myth from memory. Wry, rambling and tender, it was co-written with playwright Sam Shepard and runs past eleven minutes, with backing singers answering his lines.
driftin-too-far-from-shore: The singer tells a lover that she has wandered so far from him that there may be no bringing her back. He sounds frustrated and a little bitter, puzzled by her moods and tired of trying, though he cannot quite let her go. The verses circle the same distance between them rather than telling a story, and the tone stays restless throughout. It is one of the few songs on the album Dylan wrote by himself.
they-killed-him: This is Dylan's version of a Kris Kristofferson song. Each verse remembers a man who preached peace and love, Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr. and Jesus, and each ends the same way, with the man cut down by violence. The repetition turns three life stories into one lament about how the world treats those who ask it to be better. Dylan sings it plainly and earnestly, with a children's choir joining him.
death-is-not-the-end: The singer speaks to someone overwhelmed by sorrow, fear and confusion, whose hopes have collapsed and who no longer knows whom to trust. Verse by verse he names more of the world's troubles, from crime to loneliness, then answers each with the same steady reassurance that death does not have the final word. The tone is grave and consoling rather than triumphant. It was an outtake from the 1983 Infidels sessions, sung slowly and solemnly.
rank-strangers-to-me: In this Albert E. Brumley song, best known from the Stanley Brothers, a man returns to the place where he grew up hoping to find old friends. Everyone he meets is a stranger, and he slowly realizes that the people he knew are gone. In the end he takes comfort in the hope of meeting them again in a life beyond this one. Dylan sings it slowly and simply, letting the loneliness of the story carry it.
silvio: A restless narrator announces that he is setting out to learn what fate holds for him, ready to take whatever he finds. The verses are boastful and a bit cryptic, full of hints at trouble and mystery, while the chorus turns his search into a journey toward knowledge the living do not have. The tone is swaggering and carefree. Written with Grateful Dead lyricist Robert Hunter, it is an upbeat rocker that became a regular in his concerts.
everything-is-broken: The singer reels off a long, rolling list of things that no longer work, from household objects and machinery to laws, promises and people. The catalogue starts small and keeps widening until the whole world seems to be coming apart, yet the delivery is wry rather than despairing, almost a shrug. There is no story, just the steady pile-up of damage. It was released as a single with a music video and moves on a swampy, rhythmic groove.
man-in-the-long-black-coat: A woman has gone off with a mysterious stranger, and the song sketches the empty, uneasy place she left behind. The singer gathers fragments: a sermon about conscience, rumors, the silent landscape, and the lingering question of whether she was lured away or went willingly. Nothing is explained, and the stranger remains a shadow. The recording opens with the sound of crickets, adding to Daniel Lanois's swampy, dreamlike atmosphere.
most-of-the-time: The singer insists he has moved on from a past love: he is clear-headed, steady, and hardly thinks of her at all. Yet every claim of calm comes with the same small qualifier, and the more he repeats it, the more obvious it becomes that he has not let go. The tone is soft and self-deceiving, which makes it quietly sad. The slow, atmospheric track was used in the 2000 film High Fidelity.
political-world: The singer describes a world where politics governs everything and leaves no room for wisdom, love, mercy or peace. Each verse adds another virtue that has been pushed aside or locked away, building a picture of a society that has lost its moral center. The tone is blunt and bleak, delivered with steady force rather than outrage. The opening track sets the album's mood of a corrupt world, on a driving, insistent rhythm.
ring-them-bells: The singer calls for bells to ring out across a world that seems close to its end, on behalf of the lost, the blind, the faithful and those who have been forgotten. Each verse widens the circle of who needs to hear them, mixing sorrow with a stubborn hope. The tone is solemn and prayerful. It is a slow, hymn-like song built around piano, one of the most quietly moving moments on the album.
shooting-star: The singer sees a star fall across the night sky and thinks of a woman he once loved, wondering whether he ever became the man she hoped for or simply let her down. From there the song widens into a sense of last things: chances closing, an ending drawing near, one final call to change. Its tone is gentle and regretful rather than bitter, and as the closing track of Oh Mercy it leaves the album on a quiet, reflective note.
what-good-am-i: Speaking to himself, the singer asks a string of hard questions about his own conduct. Would he be worth anything if he looked away from people in need, kept silent when he should speak, or shut himself off from the pain around him? Each verse adds another test of conscience, and none is answered outright, so the listener is left to weigh them too. It is one of the quietest songs on Oh Mercy, sung softly over a hushed, sparse backing.
born-in-time: A man looks back on a love affair as if through a haze of memory, recalling how it began and how it seemed to belong to its own particular moment. He speaks to the woman directly, tender but aware that what they shared has passed. The verses drift between closeness and distance, dream and recollection, and the mood is wistful rather than angry. Dylan first tried the song during the Oh Mercy sessions before it appeared on Under the Red Sky.
under-the-red-sky: Told like a fairy tale, the song follows a boy and a girl who live in a little town, and the singer seems to address one of them as if recalling a shared childhood. Its simple, riddling verses hint at danger beneath the surface, and by the end the place and its innocence are gone and the world they knew has come undone. The childlike telling makes the sadness underneath feel stranger. George Harrison adds slide guitar to the title track.
wiggle-wiggle: In a nursery-rhyme chant, the singer keeps telling someone to wiggle, piling up nonsense comparisons that grow odder and slightly more menacing as they go. There is no real story, only a run of playful commands repeated with cheerful insistence. The song works more as a rhythm and a mood than as a message, a deliberately silly opener. It starts Under the Red Sky, with Slash of Guns N' Roses playing guitar.
arthur-mcbride: The narrator tells of a morning stroll with his cousin Arthur McBride, when the two meet a sergeant, a corporal and a young drummer out recruiting. The sergeant tempts them with talk of pay, fine clothes and glory, but the cousins reply that they know what soldiering really costs. When the recruiters turn threatening, the pair beat them soundly and send them off. Dylan sings this Irish anti-recruiting song alone with his acoustic guitar, having learned it from Paul Brady's recording.
frankie-and-albert: This old murder ballad follows Frankie, who loves Albert devotedly until she learns he has been seeing another woman. She goes after him with a gun and shoots him, and then the law and its judgment close in on her. Each verse moves the story forward plainly, with a refrain that keeps returning to her sense of betrayal. Dylan's version opens Good as I Been to You, sung alone with acoustic guitar in a brisk, matter-of-fact way.
froggie-went-a-courtin: In this centuries-old children's song, a frog rides out to court a mouse, asks her uncle for permission to marry, and a wedding feast follows with a parade of animal guests. The festivities end in chaos when hungry predators arrive and scatter the party. Dylan tells the tale patiently, verse after verse, treating its nonsense with a straight face that makes it both funny and faintly sad. Sung alone over acoustic guitar, it closes the album at more than six minutes.
delia: Drawn from the real 1900 killing of a teenage girl in Savannah, Georgia, the song tells of Delia, shot by the young man who loved her. The verses move from the shooting to the courtroom and on to the prison cell, where he is left with nothing but his regret. Between them a mournful refrain grieves for friends who are gone. Dylan sings it slowly and plainly with acoustic guitar, letting the sorrow carry the story rather than the drama.
stack-a-lee: The ballad retells the 1895 St. Louis killing of Billy Lyons by Lee Shelton, the man remembered as Stack a Lee. A quarrel over a hat turns deadly when Stack a Lee shoots Billy, who begs to be spared for the sake of his family. The story then follows the killer into the hands of the law, while the song turns him into a legend, part villain and part folk hero. Dylan performs it alone with acoustic guitar in a steady, unhurried telling.
world-gone-wrong: Speaking to a lover, the singer explains that he can no longer behave as he once did, because the whole world around him has gone wrong. The verses touch on broken trust, trouble at home and his resolve to leave, each one returning to the same weary refrain. The tone is resigned rather than angry, more a shrug at ruin than a protest. The song comes from the Mississippi Sheiks, and Dylan performs it alone with acoustic guitar.
cold-irons-bound: A man walks away from a love that has turned against him, feeling as though he is being hauled off in chains. The verses mix memories of the woman with images of a bleak, windswept country and a growing sense that the world he trusted has betrayed him. The refrain keeps returning him to his captivity, far from where he wants to be. The band plays a dark, pounding groove drenched in echo, and the song won the 1998 Grammy for Best Male Rock Vocal Performance.
highlands: Over a long, loping blues, a man drifts through an ordinary city day while his mind keeps returning to the highlands, a distant place where he feels he truly belongs. He watches people pass, grumbles about the times, and stops in a restaurant, where a waitress asks him to draw her and their exchange turns wry and prickly. The tone is dry, funny and weary all at once. At more than sixteen minutes it closes Time Out of Mind.
love-sick: A man walks through streets that feel empty and hostile, worn down by a love he wishes he had never known yet cannot give up. He sees couples around him and feels only the distance between himself and them. The verses circle the same restless mood, contradictory, weary and sick at heart, without offering relief. As the opening track of Time Out of Mind, it sets the album's dark, spare tone with a flickering organ and a slow, stalking beat.
make-you-feel-my-love: The singer speaks to someone he loves and promises to comfort them through any hardship, offering shelter, patience and steady devotion. Each verse adds another pledge of what he would do and endure for them, and he insists he knew from the start that they belonged together. The language is simple and the feeling direct, closer to a hymn than a confession. Billy Joel released a version before Dylan's own, and it became one of his most covered songs.
not-dark-yet: An aging man takes stock of a life that is wearing out, admitting that he feels detached from the world and weighed down by everything he has seen and lost. The verses move slowly and evenly, each one coming back to the sense that the end is close but has not quite arrived. He speaks of failed love, of travel, and of understanding little more now than before. The tone is resigned and unhurried, sad without self-pity.
standing-in-the-doorway: Left by a lover, the singer stands at a threshold, unsure whether to stay where she left him or move on. Over nearly eight minutes he drifts through memories, the small sounds of the night and flashes of bitterness, yet keeps returning to a love that will not fade. He insists he will get by, though he never sounds certain of it. The ballad moves slowly and loosely, matching the singer's hesitation.
tryin-to-get-to-heaven: A weary traveler passes through river towns, trains and stations, and every stop reminds him how far he still is from where he hopes to end up. The verses gather scenes from an old American landscape of journeys and departures, and the people he meets offer little comfort. The refrain holds on to his goal of reaching salvation while there is still time. The tone is tired but steady, and Dylan reshaped the song often in concert in the years after the album came out.
high-water-for-charley-patton: As floodwaters rise across the South, the singer surveys a scene of panic and ruin, crowded with blues singers, figures from old songs and stray characters each facing the deluge. The verses are fragmentary and ominous, threaded with dark humor and hints of judgment, and nobody seems sure where safety lies. A driving banjo pushes the band forward. The song is dedicated to the Delta blues pioneer Charley Patton, who sang of an earlier great flood.
honest-with-me: Trapped in a town he despises, an uneasy man presses his companion to stop lying to him. He swings between boasts, threats, jokes and complaints, never settling long enough to explain himself, and the verses pile up odd details of his discontent. The refrain keeps pressing for straight talk he does not seem to expect. It is a hard-driving electric blues built on a slide-guitar riff, loud and relentless.
mississippi: Having lingered somewhere past his time, a man reviews the mistakes and missed chances of his life. He speaks to a woman, admitting what he has lost and how little he can change, yet he still offers her his love and refuses to call himself finished. The verses mix regret with a weathered dignity. Dylan first tried the song during the Time Out of Mind sessions, and Sheryl Crow released a version before his own appeared.
po-boy: A poor wanderer drifts from one odd scene to the next, from cheap lodgings to strange family dramas, meeting each setback with a joke. The verses are full of wordplay, puns and old vaudeville gags, so that hardship and comedy sit side by side. Beneath the humor is a picture of someone with little to his name who keeps going anyway. The tune is light and jazzy, played gently with a relaxed, old-fashioned swing.
sugar-baby: A world-weary man addresses a woman he calls Sugar Baby, telling her the old days are gone and that she should face what is coming. He looks over a dry, broken world full of hard lessons and false hopes, and warns her to make her peace before judgment arrives. His tone is tender and stern at once, more sorrowful than scolding. The slow, brooding closing track runs well over six minutes.
summer-days: Refusing to accept that his best years are spent, an aging man boasts, jokes, flirts with a woman and argues with anyone who claims the past cannot be lived again, while hints of age and loss slip in at the edges. The verses tumble out quickly, mixing swagger with sly self-mockery. It is a fast jump-blues number that became a lively fixture of his concerts.
tweedle-dee-and-tweedle-dum: A pair of near-identical partners travel through a sideshow version of America, inseparable and indistinguishable. The verses suggest plots, deceptions and crimes without ever explaining them, and the pair seem as wary of each other as of the world. The mood is comic but uneasy, a picture of shared ambition and mutual suspicion. The opening track borrows its title characters from the old English nursery rhyme also used by Lewis Carroll.
aint-talkin: A solitary traveler trudges across a broken, unfriendly landscape, refusing to share what is on his mind. He passes through gardens and fields nursing old wounds and grudges, swinging between prayer in one moment and thoughts of revenge in the next. The refrain returns again and again to his silence and his walking. At almost nine minutes it is the somber closer of Modern Times, slow and steady.
rollin-and-tumblin: A restless man wakes early, unable to rest, and wrestles with his troubles and with a woman who has treated him badly. The verses complain, threaten and boast in turn, but the song is driven more by its rolling rhythm than by any story. Dylan built it on the old Delta blues tune best known from Muddy Waters' 1950 recording, and the band plays it as a loud, churning electric blues.
someday-baby: Tired of being treated badly, a man warns his lover that a time is coming when her cruelty will no longer reach him. He lists her faults and his own frustrations, more weary than furious, and seems to be talking himself into leaving as much as warning her. The verses move at an easy, shuffling pace. It won the 2007 Grammy for Best Solo Rock Vocal Performance.
spirit-on-the-water: Barred for good from paradise, a man remains unable to stop dreaming of the woman he adores. He confesses his longing and his past mistakes, mixing tender declarations with jokes and boasts about himself, and wonders whether she feels the same. The song takes its time, letting the verses wander. It is a gentle, swinging love song that runs more than seven minutes.
thunder-on-the-mountain: The singer watches a great disturbance gathering over the country and braces himself to meet it. The verses mix apocalyptic images with wisecracks, boasts and odd asides, so that dread and good humor run side by side. He seems both to welcome the coming upheaval and to stand apart from it. The opening track of Modern Times moves at a brisk, rollicking pace, and it famously name-checks the singer Alicia Keys.
when-the-deal-goes-down: Thinking about how short and uncertain life is, a man promises the person he loves that he will be beside her at the finish. The verses are calm and measured, touching on the limits of knowledge, the passing of time and the comfort of love that remains. The tone is tender and accepting rather than fearful. It is a slow waltz in the style of the old crooner ballads.
workingmans-blues-2: A working man speaks to the woman he loves while the economy turns against people like him: pay shrinks, jobs vanish and the powerful seem untouchable. The verses drift between plain talk about hardship, battlefield imagery, memories and tender promises, always circling back to a refrain that holds on to her as his anchor. The tone is weary but proud rather than bitter. It moves at a gentle, unhurried pace, led by piano and a soft band.
here-comes-santa-claus: Dylan plays the old holiday standard completely straight, announcing Santa's arrival as if passing on good news to the neighborhood. The verses picture the sleigh, the reindeer and children getting ready for bed, then widen into a note of goodwill that reminds listeners Santa treats everyone alike and that the season has a religious root. His rough, worn voice sits against a bright, old-fashioned arrangement with a warm backing chorus, which gives the cheer an oddly touching sincerity.
must-be-santa: This is a call-and-response game in which one voice asks a string of questions about a mysterious visitor and the answers pile up until there is only one possible guest. Each round adds another clue and repeats the earlier ones, so the song keeps speeding up and growing sillier as it goes. Dylan treats it as pure fun, roaring through a frantic polka with accordion and a crowd of party voices shouting the replies.
the-christmas-blues: Someone spends the holidays alone and finds that everything meant to bring joy only reminds them of what is missing. The verses walk through familiar seasonal sights and sounds, the decorations, the music, the good wishes of others, and set each against the speaker's empty feeling. There is no turn toward comfort; the song simply sits with the sadness. Dylan sings it slowly and quietly, letting the bluesy mood hang over the festive setting.
beyond-here-lies-nothin: The singer addresses his lover as they move through a dark, deserted night, and he tells her that what they share is all there is; past it there is only emptiness. The verses sketch empty streets, closed doors and a sense of time running out, but the mood is tough and determined rather than despairing. The refrain lands like a vow. A rolling, Latin-flavored groove with prominent accordion gives the song a smoky, border-town swagger.
i-feel-a-change-comin-on: An older man, half amused at himself, senses that something in his life is about to shift and hopes it will finally bring him the woman he has been watching. The verses wander through his days, his reading and his music, with a wry aside about the country singer Billy Joe Shaver, before returning to the feeling of change in the air. The tone is relaxed and teasing, carried by an easy, loping band sound.
life-is-hard: A lonely man moves through his days without the person he lost, and everything around him feels heavier for her absence. The verses are quiet and plain, describing evenings, memories and a resolve to keep going even though the world has grown harder to face alone. There is no dramatic turn, only a steady, resigned tenderness. Dylan croons it softly as a slow ballad, closer to an old-fashioned love song than to the bluesier tracks around it.
duquesne-whistle: A train whistle sounds through the night as the singer travels toward home and the woman he loves, and the sound seems to carry both promise and warning. The verses mix romantic longing with hints of trouble along the line, so the cheerful surface never quite settles. After a mock-vintage swing opening that sounds like an old record, the full band kicks in and the song rolls along at a bright, rocking pace.
roll-on-john: Dylan speaks directly to John Lennon, following him from his youth in Liverpool through the clubs of Hamburg, worldwide fame and his later life in New York, up to his sudden death. The verses mix scenes from Lennon's life with echoes of his own songs and of older poetry, while the refrain keeps urging him onward into whatever lies beyond. The tone is tender and mournful, set to a slow, hymn-like accompaniment that closes the album.
tempest: This long narrative ballad retells the Titanic's last night, moving among passengers and crew as they dance, gamble, pray and face the end. There is no chorus; verse follows verse like an old folk ballad, returning to a watchman who dreams the disaster as it happens, and it even nods to the famous film. The tone is calm and fatalistic. It unfolds as a lilting waltz with fiddle and accordion, steady and almost soothing despite the subject.
full-moon-and-empty-arms: A lover alone under a bright moon spends the night wishing the absent person were there, and turns the moonlight into a kind of promise that they will be together again. The song moves from longing toward hope, ending on a quiet wish rather than despair. Dylan sings the old standard with a small, hushed band, where gentle pedal steel takes the place of the lush strings of the classic versions.
im-a-fool-to-want-you: The singer confesses that he cannot stop longing for someone who has treated him badly, and he knows full well that the desire is foolish. The verses move between self-reproach and helpless need, never resolving the conflict, which is what gives the torch song its ache. Opening the album, Dylan sings it slowly and close to the microphone, with a sparse band and mournful pedal steel leaving plenty of space around his voice.
that-lucky-old-sun: A worn-out laborer describes a life of toil for his family and his Lord, and compares himself bitterly with the sun, which crosses the sky every day without any burden. As the song goes on, his envy turns into a weary prayer for release and rest. The tone is tired but dignified, close to a spiritual. Closing the album, Dylan delivers it slowly, with a spare band behind him and the final lines left to linger.
all-the-way: The singer offers a love that holds nothing back, promising devotion that will last through good fortune and hard times alike. The verses explain what such love asks of a person, steady and unconditional rather than half-hearted, and the song builds gently toward its title as a final pledge. Dylan's aged voice gives the romantic standard a thoughtful, lived-in quality, backed by a small, quiet band in place of the big orchestra of earlier versions.
melancholy-mood: Someone sunk in gloom after a love has ended admits that the sadness has settled in and will not lift. The singer describes the low feeling and longs for the day the clouds part and happiness returns, so the song hangs between despair and a faint hope. Dylan sings the old standard with a light, swaying touch, and the small band keeps the melancholy soft rather than heavy.
young-at-heart: The song argues that staying hopeful, playful and open to wonder keeps a person young, whatever the calendar says. Its verses list the rewards of that outlook, from dreams that come true to a longer, happier life, and the cheerful message builds to a gentle conclusion. Coming from Dylan in his seventies, the advice sounds wistful as much as sunny. It opens the album at an easy, swaying pace with a soft small-band backing.
as-time-goes-by: The singer reflects that whatever else in the world changes, the basic facts of love stay the same, and the old gestures between lovers keep their meaning. The song moves from these general truths to a hope that love will last against everything, ending on a note of quiet confidence. Dylan sings the standard from Casablanca tenderly and unhurriedly, with a light, understated band behind him.
september-of-my-years: A man in the autumn of his life looks back over the seasons of his years, weighing the joys and regrets they held. The verses move between fond memory and sober acceptance, treating age as both a loss and a kind of ripening. The tone is reflective and bittersweet rather than sad. Dylan's weathered voice suits the theme, and he sings it slowly over a soft, spare arrangement.
stormy-weather: Since the singer's lover left, it feels as though the rain has never stopped, and the gloom outside mirrors the gloom within. The verses describe a life gone gray, weariness and the hope that the sun will someday return with the lost love. The tone is heavy and patient, a slow lament rather than an outburst. Dylan takes the famous standard at a gentle, unhurried pace with a small band.
crossing-the-rubicon: A man announces that he has made his irreversible choice and will not turn back, taking the ancient image of Caesar's crossing as his own. The verses swing between prayer, menace, dark humor and glimpses of his past, so it is never clear whether he is a pilgrim or a threat. Each verse ends by returning to the decision he has made. It grinds along as a slow, heavy blues, menacing and steady.
false-prophet: A defiant speaker insists that he is genuine, no fake, and warns off his enemies with a mix of boasting and grim humor. The verses pile up claims about his strength, his past and his readiness to face death, sounding at once like a gunfighter and an old preacher. The tone is swaggering and sardonic. Its music is built on Billy Emerson's 1954 Sun Records blues, played as a slow, snarling electric shuffle.
goodbye-jimmy-reed: Dylan bids farewell to the Chicago blues man Jimmy Reed, mixing praise for him with scenes of rough living, church and loyalty to the music. The verses jump between religion, violence and memories of hearing the blues, as if the speaker were explaining where his own life and faith came from. The tone is affectionate and rowdy. It rocks along as a lively, stomping blues that echoes Reed's own style.
i-contain-multitudes: An aging narrator describes himself as a bundle of contradictions, holding many selves and moods at once. The verses work like a self-portrait made of opposites and borrowed figures, naming people from Anne Frank and Indiana Jones to the Rolling Stones, as he admits to both tenderness and menace. The tone is calm, sly and quietly unsettling. It is a soft, almost hushed performance over gentle guitar, letting each verse unfold slowly.
key-west-philosopher-pirate: The narrator tells of the island city at the tip of Florida as a dreamlike refuge, a place where he finds healing and peace at the end of the road.
