The verses drift through memories of radio, poets, a presidential assassination and his own wanderings, always returning to the island in the refrain. The tone is gentle and wistful, like a slow dream. Running over nine minutes, it floats along with accordion throughout.
murder-most-foul: The killing of John F. Kennedy in Dallas in 1963 is retold in close, haunting detail, as if the event had never finished happening. Midway, the song widens into a long request to a disc jockey, calling up songs, films and performers of the era, so the national tragedy and its soundtrack become tangled together. The tone is solemn and incantatory. Nearly seventeen minutes long, it unfolds slowly over piano and strings with almost no beat.
my-own-version-of-you: In the manner of Frankenstein, a narrator roams graveyards and history gathering body parts and borrowed qualities to build himself the perfect companion. The verses list the pieces he wants, drawn from famous figures and stories, and the project grows stranger and more macabre as it goes, while the speaker remains oddly calm. The tone is darkly comic and eerie. It moves at a slow, creeping pace with a menacing, low-lit band sound.
someones-got-a-hold-of-my-heart: The speaker is caught in a love he cannot shake, haunted by a woman who seems to have power over him and feeling watched and unsettled wherever he goes. The verses move through restless nights and vague threats, with the title returning as a confession of helplessness. The tone is brooding and tense. This Infidels outtake is the earlier version of the song that he later reworked for Empire Burlesque.
youre-no-good: A lover's grievance played for laughs: the singer lists the ways a woman has treated him badly and decides she is simply no good. It moves fast, with little build, each verse another complaint thrown off with a grin. Dylan's version is loose and rough-voiced, a young singer hamming up an older man's blues. It sets the tone for an album of borrowed songs sung with more nerve than polish.
in-my-time-of-dyin: A deathbed song: the speaker faces his last hour and asks that heaven make his passing easy. It is built on repetition, the same plea returning as the verses circle the moment of death. Dylan sings it with a hoarse urgency far older than his years, over a sliding, moaning guitar line. Like much of the album, it shows a twenty-year-old singer drawn again and again to songs about dying.
man-of-constant-sorrow: The speaker is a man marked by sorrow all his life, about to leave the place he grew up and go wandering. It unfolds as a farewell, each verse another goodbye to home, friends and a sweetheart he may never see again. Dylan slows it down and sings it with a mournful drawl over guitar and harmonica, turning a mountain lament into something closer to a blues.
fixin-to-die: The singer feels death coming and cannot stop thinking about it, though what troubles him most is leaving his children alone. The verses return to that one fear with little relief, the beat driving on as if there were no time to waste. Dylan attacks it with a rasping, exaggerated growl and hard-strummed guitar, one of the most intense performances on a record full of songs about mortality.
pretty-peggy-o: An old soldier's ballad: a captain passing through a town falls for a local girl and asks her to come away with him, but she turns him down. The story moves quickly from courtship to his death far away. Dylan sings it with a mock-hillbilly swagger and whoops, treating a sad old ballad almost as a romp, which makes its sudden ending land all the harder.
highway-51: The highway of the title runs north and south through the country, and the singer stands beside it thinking of someone who has gone. It is a road song and a lost-love song at once, the highway both what took her and what might take him. Dylan drives it hard with a pounding guitar rhythm that owes something to rockabilly, a hint of the louder music to come.
gospel-plow: A gospel song about perseverance: the believer is told to keep going, hold steady and stay fixed on the reward ahead. It draws on Bible stories in quick verses around a repeated call to hold on. Dylan turns it into a breathless, under-two-minute burst of guitar and harmonica, closer in spirit to a hoedown than a church hymn.
baby-let-me-follow-you-down: A simple, good-humoured courting song: the singer will do whatever it takes if she will just let him follow her. It repeats its single plea over a rolling fingerpicked pattern, warm rather than desperate. Dylan opens with a chatty spoken introduction crediting where he learned it, one of the few moments on the album where his offhand personality comes through between songs.
freight-train-blues: The singer was raised around trains and the railroad is in his blood; whenever a freight goes by, he has to go with it. Each verse adds more of his restless life, always ending at the pull of the tracks. Dylan sings it at a gallop with harmonica and a held, stretched-out note that shows off his lungs, a comic, high-spirited take on the hobo song.
see-that-my-grave-is-kept-clean: A man thinks about his funeral and asks only one favour of those he leaves behind: that his resting place be cared for. The song lingers on images of burial, slow and grave, with the request returning as a refrain. Dylan ends his debut with it, singing in a weary, aged voice over steady guitar, a final note on the album's preoccupation with death.
down-the-highway: The singer's woman has gone overseas and taken his heart with her, and all he can do is walk the road alone. It is a straight twelve-bar blues in form, with verses that move between loneliness and grim humour. Dylan plays it with a hard, choppy guitar and sings in a tough, clipped voice, a personal blues dressed in the traditional style he had been studying.
bob-dylans-blues: After a deadpan spoken introduction mocking the songwriting factories of New York, Dylan offers a loose, improvised-sounding song about himself. Its verses wander through jokes and small boasts, with no real story and no pretensions. Played on guitar with harmonica, it sounds tossed off in a single take, a breather between the heavier songs on the album.
talking-world-war-iii-blues: Framed as a visit to a psychiatrist, the song recounts a dream in which the speaker survives atomic war and roams a deserted America looking for anyone else alive. It is told in the half-spoken talking-blues form, each episode ending on a punchline. The comedy carries real Cold War dread underneath, and the ending turns the joke on the listener: everyone, it seems, is having the same nightmare.
corrina-corrina: The singer's lover is gone, and the song is his gentle, persistent wish that she would return. It moves through a few short verses with the same yearning refrain, never angry, only patient and sad. Dylan sings it softly over a quiet band shuffle, a warm, unhurried recording that stands out among the album's solo performances.
honey-just-allow-me-one-more-chance: The singer asks to be forgiven and taken back, though he sounds more cheerful than repentant. It is brief and bouncing, little more than a refrain and a couple of verses, with whoops and harmonica breaks between them. Dylan plays it for fun, the kind of jaunty old-time number that lightened his live sets of the time.
i-shall-be-free: A series of absurd vignettes: the singer finds himself in improbable situations with famous and ordinary people, each verse ending in a punchline. Between them a refrain promises that he will be free. The tone is satirical and goofy, poking at the news and the culture of the early sixties. It ends the album on a laugh after its protests and love songs.
all-i-really-want-to-do: The singer runs through a long list of things he will not do to the woman he is addressing, all the ways he will not try to change, trap or own her. The list keeps growing, each line a playful denial, before returning to the simple refrain of what he does want. Dylan sings it with yodels and laughter breaking through, a buoyant opening that announces the lighter, more personal record.
black-crow-blues: The singer is restless and alone, missing a woman who is not coming back soon, and everything around him seems to mirror his gloom. The song circles in short verses with harmonica breaks, a mood more than a story. Dylan plays a rolling, barrelhouse-style piano, giving the record an unexpected texture between its guitar songs.
spanish-harlem-incident: The singer is captivated by a woman in Spanish Harlem, and the song is his rush of attraction, part flirtation and part surrender. It is brief and impressionistic, three verses of heat and colour with no resolution. Dylan sings it quickly over guitar, a sketch of infatuation rather than a story.
i-shall-be-free-no-10: Like its predecessor, it strings together absurd scenes and wisecracks, each verse a fresh joke about boxing, politics, fame or his neighbours. There is no plot, just a running stream of nonsense delivered with a straight face and a refrain of freedom. Dylan plays it on guitar and harmonica, sounding relaxed and amused, a sign of the less earnest songwriter on this album.
to-ramona: The singer addresses a woman who is unhappy and confused, pulled by voices telling her how to live. He offers comfort and advice, but admits he may be no wiser, and in the end leaves the choice to her. The song sways in three-four time with a soft, consoling tone. It is one of Dylan's most tender early songs, sung quietly over a swaying guitar.
motorpsycho-nitemare: A wanderer knocks at a farmhouse door and is given shelter on condition he leaves the daughter alone. Things go wrong from there in a chain of slapstick events, with nods to horror films and Cold War politics along the way. It is told in a fast, half-spoken style with harmonica, a satire of small-town suspicion played entirely for laughs.
i-dont-believe-you-she-acts-like-we-neve: The singer cannot understand the cold shoulder he is getting from a woman who, not long ago, was close to him. He moves between hurt, disbelief and wry humour, going over what happened and what has changed. The original is a brisk acoustic performance with a catch in the voice, wry rather than bitter.
ballad-in-plain-d: A narrative song looking back at a broken relationship: the singer tells how he fell for a young woman, how tensions with her family grew, and how a final fight ended it. It runs through many verses in a slow, steady waltz, more diary than ballad. The tone is raw and self-accusing, with a closing reflection on whether he is truly free. Its bluntness makes it one of his most personal early songs.
one-too-many-mornings: The singer stands at the edge of a parting, looking back at the house and the woman he is leaving as night turns to morning. There is no quarrel and no blame; each verse settles on the idea that two people can both be right and still be finished. The mood is tired and tender rather than bitter. Dylan sings it softly over his guitar, with harmonica breaks that stretch the stillness.
north-country-blues: A woman tells her own life story from childhood to middle age in a northern mining town. Her family is lost one by one, her husband's work disappears when the company finds cheaper ore abroad, and her household slowly empties. The song moves in plain, unhurried verses, each a step further into hardship, with no chorus to relieve it. Dylan sings it alone with guitar, in a flat, steady voice that lets the story carry the anger.
she-belongs-to-me: Despite its title, the song is about a woman nobody can own. The singer describes an artist who answers to herself alone, who sees through everyone around her and keeps them at a distance, while he and others hover around her in admiration and some fear. The tone is wry and affectionate, with a hint of mockery aimed at the men who court her. The gentle electric backing and harmonica make it one of the album's calmest moments.
outlaw-blues: The singer pictures himself as an outlaw, on the run and on edge, keeping his head down and his guard up. The verses are a string of half-comic, half-menacing images rather than a story, delivered in a loose twelve-bar shape. Dylan sounds gleeful in the role, growling over a stomping band. The guitar is ragged and the rhythm heavy, and the whole thing has the feel of a live take caught on the run.
on-the-road-again: The singer describes visiting the home of the woman he is seeing, where every room and every relative is stranger than the last. Each verse piles up another grotesque or ridiculous detail of the family's daily life, and each ends with him turning to her in disbelief at the idea that he could live there. It is a comic song, close to a cartoon, sung with mock exasperation over a jaunty, rattling band and bursts of harmonica.
bob-dylans-115th-dream: The song is a long comic tall tale in which the narrator sails to America, steps ashore and stumbles from one misadventure to the next, meeting a string of hostile, greedy or baffling locals before fleeing back to sea. It plays on the story of discovery, turning the arrival in the New World into slapstick. The verses tumble on without a chorus, and Dylan sings it with a grin over a loose, galloping band after the opening breakdown.
it-takes-a-lot-to-laugh-it-takes-a-train: The singer is on the move, tired and far from home, and the train becomes the image for his longing and his patience. Rather than a story, the verses gather railway and nighttime pictures around a quiet wish to reach the woman waiting for him. The tone is relaxed and a little melancholy, a pause after the album's harder songs. A rolling piano and an easy shuffle give it the feel of an old blues record.
from-a-buick-6: The singer describes a woman who is his refuge in a rough world, someone who protects and steadies him while everything around him threatens. The verses are a series of quick, tough images of danger and death, each turning back to her loyalty. It is boastful and grateful at once, more celebration than romance. The band races through it with a driving organ and bass, and Dylan's harmonica squeals over the top.
pledging-my-time: The singer speaks to a woman he wants, offering her his loyalty while hinting at the trouble and sickness all around him. The song is a slow, swaggering blues built on repeated pledges, with dark asides about danger slipping between them. The mood is smoky and late-night rather than romantic. Electric guitar and heavy drums lumber along, and Dylan's harmonica wails between the verses.
one-of-us-must-know-sooner-or-later: The singer looks back on a relationship that ended badly and tries to set the record straight with the woman he hurt. He insists he did not understand her and did not mean what she took from him, while admitting she saw through him. Each verse builds to a big, pleading chorus. The sound swells from a quiet start into a crashing wall of piano, organ and drums, with Dylan straining against it.
leopard-skin-pill-box-hat: The singer fixes on a woman's fashionable hat and turns it into a running joke about vanity, status and his own jealousy. Each verse finds him admiring, envying or teasing her as she moves on to someone else, always circling back to the hat. It is pure comedy, sharp but not cruel. The band plays a stinging, stop-start blues with stabbing electric guitar, and Dylan delivers it with deadpan timing.
most-likely-you-go-your-way-and-ill-go-m: The singer has had enough of a relationship full of games and false promises, and he says so plainly. The verses list her tricks and his tiredness, and the chorus answers each with the same cool conclusion that they should part. It is less heartbroken than relieved, with a cocky, almost cheerful air. A brassy, stomping arrangement with horns punching the rhythm makes the farewell sound like a celebration.
temporary-like-achilles: The singer stands outside a woman's door, wanting to be let in and growing weary of her coldness. He describes her as hard to reach and protected by a rival who acts as her guard, someone only briefly invincible. The song is a lament with a sly wit, moving at a slow, rolling pace. A barrelhouse piano leads the way, with harmonica answering Dylan's drawled, frustrated vocal.
absolutely-sweet-marie: The singer has been waiting for a woman who never shows up, and the song is a string of his complaints and puzzled questions. The images are of being locked out, held up and left behind, mixed with odd pieces of wisdom about honesty and living by your own rules. Despite the frustration, the mood is bright and energetic. A pumping organ and quick beat drive it, and Dylan's harmonica rings out between verses.
obviously-five-believers: This is one of the simplest songs on the album, a straight call to a woman to return to him. The singer begs, coaxes and reassures, with each verse repeating his longing over a tight, insistent groove. It draws openly on the Chicago electric blues records of the 1950s. Driving guitar riffs and a shrill harmonica keep it tense and fast, and the band sounds loose and joyful.
the-ballad-of-frankie-lee-and-judas-prie: The song tells the story of two friends: a gambler and a cunning companion who offers him money and leads him toward a house of temptation. The gambler gives in, and his craving costs him his life, while his friend watches. It unfolds like a biblical parable or an old ballad, verse after verse without a chorus, before closing with a plainly stated lesson. Dylan sings it at a brisk, even pace over guitar, bass and drums.
dear-landlord: The singer addresses a landlord, though the figure seems to stand for anyone with a hold over him. He asks for patience and fair treatment, admits his own weaknesses, and suggests that both of them are struggling in their own ways. The tone is calm, dignified and slightly weary, more a request for mutual respect than a protest. Dylan's piano and a plain rhythm section give it a hymn-like steadiness.
i-am-a-lonesome-hobo: The narrator is a homeless wanderer who once had wealth and status and lost everything through his own dishonesty and greed. He looks back without self-pity and turns his story into advice for whoever is listening, urging honesty and generosity. It moves like a sermon in miniature, steady and grave. The spare backing of acoustic guitar, bass, drums and harmonica keeps the focus on the confession.
i-pity-the-poor-immigrant: The singer looks with pity, not anger, on an immigrant who arrives seeking a better life but lives only for gain and harms others along the way. The verses list his failings in a solemn, almost biblical voice, and the song suggests his dreams will bring him no peace. Its mood is mournful and reflective, a moral portrait more than a story. Dylan sings it slowly over acoustic guitar and harmonica.
down-along-the-cove: After an album of dark parables, the singer suddenly sounds content: he is out walking with his lover and delighted to be seen with her. There is no conflict, only simple affection and pride. It is a short, easy blues with a cheerful lope and a country lilt. Dylan's piano and the pedal steel guitar give it a relaxed, sunny warmth that points toward his next album.
peggy-day: The singer sings the praises of a girl named Peggy, cheerfully admitting how much he enjoys her company. There is no conflict and no heartbreak, only a happy man trading a couple of verses of good-humoured devotion. Its bouncy rhythm and slightly old-fashioned, music-hall feel make it one of the sunniest moments on the album. The ending shifts into a slower, mock-grand coda that adds a wink to the whole thing.
one-more-night: The singer is out under a clear, moonlit sky, but the beauty of the night only reminds him that his love has gone. He blames himself for not being the kind of man she needed, and the song circles back to his solitude. The words are sad, yet the band plays a quick, cheerful country shuffle, so grief and good spirits sit side by side. It is a short, plain-spoken lament in classic country style.
country-pie: This is a song of pure enjoyment: the singer declares his appetite for country pie, reeling off one kind of fruit after another. The pie works as a cheerful metaphor for the down-home music and easy living he loves, and he wants nothing fancier. It moves fast and never slows down, with a loose, rocking country band and a lively guitar. It is a throwaway in the best sense, a burst of fun on a gentle album.
time-passes-slowly: The singer looks at a slow, settled life in the hills, where days drift by and nothing much needs to happen. He pictures himself at home with someone he loves, far from the pressures of the wider world, and seems torn between contentment and a faint unease. The song moves at an unhurried pace, built around Dylan's own piano. It catches the domestic, rural mood that runs through New Morning.
went-to-see-the-gypsy: The singer visits a celebrated figure called the gypsy, who is staying in a grand hotel, and finds himself welcomed but uncertain what passed between them. When he returns, the gypsy has gone, and he wanders out into a quiet small-town dawn. The song has a hazy, dreamlike quality, with hints of a pilgrimage that ends in anticlimax. A rolling piano and a relaxed band keep it gently mysterious.
winterlude: Addressed to a girl the singer is courting, the song paints a cosy winter scene of snow, a chapel and evenings spent together. Its tone is warm and slightly tongue-in-cheek, like a sentimental popular song from an earlier era. Dylan sings it as a lilting waltz in a soft, crooning voice. It is one of the most deliberately gentle and nostalgic moments on New Morning, a valentine to simple happiness.
if-dogs-run-free: The song is less a story than a philosophical drift: the singer muses on letting things be as they are and on a kind of unforced harmony. Dylan delivers it in a relaxed, almost spoken style rather than a tune, sounding like a beat poet in a late-night club. Behind him, piano and brushed drums swing softly while a female singer scats freely. It is one of the strangest and most playful recordings of his early 1970s work.
new-morning: The singer greets a fresh day in the countryside, noticing small signs of life around him and feeling his spirits lift. The morning stands for a new beginning, and he shares it with someone close to him. The song builds on an exuberant, horn-touched arrangement and a big, open chorus. Its uncomplicated happiness made it the emblem of the album that critics welcomed as Dylan's return to form.
sign-on-the-window: The song opens in loneliness: rain, a deserted town and a love that has gone elsewhere. Gradually the singer turns from what he has lost toward a modest dream of marriage, children and a home far away from it all, and wonders if that might be the real meaning of happiness. Dylan sings it slowly over his own piano, and the arrangement grows fuller as hope enters. Its mood moves from melancholy to hopeful calm.
one-more-weekend: The singer is eager for a getaway with his partner, just the two of them, somewhere they can forget their responsibilities for a while. It is a playful, affectionate song about married love rather than new romance. The band plays a loose, rolling twelve-bar blues with a strutting guitar, and Dylan sings with obvious relish. Light and humorous, it shows the domestic contentment that runs through New Morning in a more raucous key.
three-angels: Dylan describes a winter street scene in a city, where three angels sit high above the sidewalk playing their horns. Below them, all kinds of people go about their business, and none seems to look up or hear. The piece asks quietly whether anyone is listening to the heavenly music around them. Delivered as a calm recitation over swelling organ and wordless voices, it sounds like a short hymn or parable.
father-of-night: The song is a hymn of praise addressed directly to God, naming him as the creator of the darkness, the seasons and the things of the earth. It draws on the shape of Jewish and Christian prayer, piling up images of creation in a steady chant. Dylan sings it over his own rolling piano with backing singers, and it lasts only about a minute and a half. It ends New Morning on a note of devotion.
alberta: This old song, sung by many folk and blues performers before Dylan, is a plea addressed to Alberta, a woman the singer misses and wants to come back to him. It is simple and repetitive, more a mood of longing than a story. Self Portrait frames the album with two different takes: the first gentle and folky with female backing voices, the second fuller and more upbeat. Both carry an easy, unhurried charm.
i-forgot-more-than-youll-ever-know: The singer addresses the person who has taken his love away, warning them that his memories of her run deeper than anything they will share. It is a classic country lament, bitter but dignified, built on a single sharp idea. Dylan sings it in the mellow, crooning voice of his Nashville period, backed by steel guitar and soft harmony vocals. His version treats it as a straightforward tribute to the country tradition he admired.
days-of-49: The song is a monologue from an aging forty-niner, recalling the gamblers, brawlers and dreamers who chased gold with him in California. One by one he tells how each came to a bad end, until he alone remains, poor and forgotten. Dylan sings it in a rough, weathered voice that suits the old man telling it. His reading leans into the ballad's mix of humour and melancholy about the American frontier.
early-mornin-rain: The singer stands on a cold, wet morning near an airfield, far from home with no money in his pocket. He watches a jet climb away and thinks of the place it is headed, where he longs to be. It is a song of homesickness and helplessness, quiet rather than angry. Dylan's version is gentle and unhurried, sung in his softer 1970 voice over acoustic guitar, staying close to the folk style of the song.
in-search-of-little-sadie: This old American ballad is narrated by the killer himself, who tells plainly how he shot Sadie, ran away and was finally arrested and sentenced. Dylan treats the song as an experiment, with the guitar and rhythm shifting abruptly so that the story seems to stagger and restart. The effect is disorienting, almost like a sketch of the song being worked out. Its companion, Little Sadie, follows later with a steadier take.
let-it-be-me: The song is a vow of devotion: the singer asks to be the one who stays by his love's side for good, offering faithfulness above everything. It is gentle and earnest, without any hint of irony. Dylan sings it softly with female backing voices, in the smooth style he adopted around Nashville Skyline. His version is a straight, affectionate tribute to a well-loved standard rather than a reinvention of it.
little-sadie: The song is a first-person confession: the narrator shoots Sadie, runs off, and is eventually tracked down and brought before a judge. He tells the story with little emotion, which makes it all the more chilling. Unlike the shifting In Search of Little Sadie, this version moves at a steady clip on acoustic guitar, much as a folk singer would play it. Placed together, the two takes show Dylan approaching the same old ballad from opposite directions.
woogie-boogie: This is a wordless jam built on the old boogie-woogie piano pattern, with the band falling in behind a steady, driving rhythm. It sounds informal, like a warm-up captured on tape rather than a polished composition. Over its brief running time it never changes much, keeping a cheerful, toe-tapping groove from start to finish. On an album full of covers and oddities, it works as a light musical interlude.
belle-isle: The song tells an old ballad story: a man meets a young woman by the shore and, without saying who he is, asks for her hand. She refuses, explaining that she is waiting for her own love, who has been away. Satisfied of her loyalty, he reveals that he is that very man. Dylan sings it slowly and tenderly, with a lush string arrangement that some listeners found surprising.
living-the-blues: The singer is lonely and lovesick, admitting that his life has been nothing but the blues since the woman he loves departed. It is a simple, sincere country lament without much story, built around one feeling. Dylan sings it in the warm, crooning voice of his Nashville period, over a relaxed band with backing voices. It sounds much like a song from the late 1950s, deliberately old-fashioned and unassuming.
gotta-travel-on: The song speaks for a wanderer who has stayed too long in one place and now hears the call to move on, despite the people he leaves behind. It is upbeat rather than mournful, treating the urge to go as part of who he is. Dylan's version is a brisk, cheerful country-folk romp with a steady beat and backing voices. It fits the album's mood of revisiting songs he had known for years.
blue-moon: This classic popular song tells of a person alone and without hope who unexpectedly finds love, as if the moon itself had answered him. It moves from loneliness to wonder in a few short verses. Dylan sings it in his gentle Nashville croon, with fiddle and a relaxed, easy backing that gives the standard a country lilt. To many listeners at the time, it was the clearest sign of how far Self Portrait strayed from expectations.
take-me-as-i-am-or-let-me-go: The singer speaks directly to a woman whose feelings for him have grown uncertain. He makes no promise to change and asks her to decide, either to take him as he stands or to release him. The song moves slowly and plainly, with a patient, pleading tone rather than anger. Dylan sings it in the smooth, crooning voice of his Nashville Skyline period, backed by easy country accompaniment.
take-a-message-to-mary: The speaker is a young outlaw who has been caught and sentenced, and will not be coming home. He sends word to his sweetheart Mary, but asks that she be told a gentler story so she can forget him and go on with her life. The song is a short, story-telling ballad with a sorrowful but restrained tone. Dylan's version keeps the country harmony feel of the original, with backing singers filling out the refrain.
it-hurts-me-too: The singer loves a woman who belongs to someone else, and that man treats her badly. He urges her to leave and come to him, insisting that whatever wounds her wounds him as well. The song follows the classic blues pattern of repeated lines and a returning refrain, sympathetic more than bitter. Dylan's version is gentle and unhurried, far from the electric slide-guitar treatment the song is best known for.
wigwam: There are no lyrics here; Dylan sings the melody as wordless syllables instead. A brass section answers him, swelling and falling in a stately, slightly woozy procession. The tune repeats in gentle circles without building to any climax, which gives it the feel of a late-night reverie or a memory of an old dance band. It is one of the few Dylan originals on Self Portrait, and its warmth has made it one of the album's best-loved tracks.
sarah-jane: The singer is a contented family man who describes his life with Sarah Jane and declares his affection for her. It plays as a light, good-humoured folk song rather than a story of trouble or heartbreak. A bouncing rhythm and a chorus of backing voices give it a loose, sing-along feel. Like the rest of the 1973 album, it was put out by Columbia from outtakes, and it sounds like a relaxed studio warm-up.
mr-bojangles: The narrator recalls a night in jail spent with an aging street performer, a dancer who has travelled the South for decades. The old man talks about his life, the dog he lost, and the drinking that keeps landing him in cells, then dances to lift the room. The song is tender and rueful, built on a gentle waltz feel. Dylan's version, cut in his 1970 sessions with backing singers, is looser and rougher than the well-known recordings.
the-ballad-of-ira-hayes: The song tells the life of Ira Hayes, a Pima man from Arizona who fought in the Pacific and was photographed raising the flag at Iwo Jima. Celebrated as a hero, he returns to a reservation stripped of its water and a nation that soon loses interest in him, and he dies alone. It unfolds as a sombre narrative ballad with a bitter refrain. Dylan's outtake, released on the 1973 album, is plain and slow, letting the story carry it.
mary-ann: The speaker is a seafaring man parted from the woman he loves, and the song dwells on his sorrow at going and his longing to return. It is a simple, lilting folk tune with a repeated chorus and a wistful tone throughout. There is little story beyond the parting itself, so the feeling rests on the melody. Dylan sings it with backing vocalists in a relaxed, unpolished arrangement typical of the outtakes Columbia gathered for this album.
big-yellow-taxi: The song looks at a landscape being covered over by development and wonders why people notice what they had only after losing it. It moves from fields, trees and birds to a more personal loss at the end, when a lover leaves. The tone is light and teasing, with a bouncing tune hiding a serious point. Dylan's version, with backing singers, is loose and playful, and he alters some of the details of Mitchell's original.
a-fool-such-as-i: The singer has been left behind, yet he cannot stop loving the woman who walked away. He addresses her directly, asking what she would want with someone so foolishly faithful, and confessing that he will love her anyway. The song is a classic country weeper, gentle and self-mocking rather than bitter. Dylan sings it in a relaxed, crooning voice over a light country backing.
spanish-is-the-loving-tongue: The speaker is a rider on the border country who recalls a brief romance with a young Mexican woman. He has long since ridden away, but the memory of her and the warmth of her language stay with him. The song is slow and melancholy, a quiet reflection rather than a story with events. Dylan's version here, from his 1969 and 1970 sessions, is a gentle, unhurried cowboy ballad.
main-title-theme-billy: This is an instrumental with no singing, written to play over the film's opening titles. Acoustic guitars state a simple, mournful melody drawn from the Billy ballad, the album's ballad about the outlaw, and other instruments join quietly around it. It keeps an even, rolling pace and never rises to a big climax. The effect is of a long, dusty ride toward something bad, which suits a film about an old friendship that ends in a killing.
cantina-theme-workin-for-the-law: There are no words here; it is a short piece of incidental music from the film. A loose rhythm and gentle guitar figures create the feel of a smoky cantina, easygoing on the surface but with an undercurrent of tension. The melody turns over and over rather than developing. Its title recalls the story at the heart of the film, of a former outlaw now working for the law and hunting his old friend.
bunkhouse-theme: This brief instrumental sets aside the drama of the film for a moment of calm. Acoustic guitars pick out a soft, folk-like melody that feels intimate and restful, as though played among friends at the end of a day. It does not build or change much, keeping one modest mood from start to finish. On the album it works as a breathing space between the more mournful themes and the songs.
river-theme: Like most of the soundtrack, it has no lyrics; voices hum and sing syllables rather than words. The music moves calmly and evenly, with a sense of drift and stillness that suits its title. Its mood is peaceful but faintly sad, a pause by the water in a story that is heading toward violence. It is a short, atmospheric piece meant to sit under a scene rather than stand alone.
turkey-chase: This is the most high-spirited piece on the soundtrack, an instrumental in the manner of a country hoedown. Fiddle and banjo trade the quick melody over a steady, galloping rhythm, giving it the feel of a frontier romp. Its playful energy stands out against the slow, mournful themes around it. As film music it suggests a moment of horseplay and freedom before the story darkens again.
final-theme: This closing instrumental gathers up the mood of the whole soundtrack. A spare, elegiac melody unfolds slowly over a gentle, steady accompaniment, with no singing. It has the feeling of an ending already decided, quiet and resigned rather than dramatic. Placed last on the album, it plays like music for the film's final scenes, after the friendship between the two men has ended in death.
going-going-gone: The singer stands at a point of no return, ready to break with a life or a love that has run its course. He speaks of leaving with a mixture of calm resolve and quiet sorrow, and a middle passage recalls advice to follow one's heart. The title phrase works as a refrain, like an auctioneer closing a sale. The Band's playing is spare and moody, with Robertson's guitar lines adding much of the song's ache.
tough-mama: The singer addresses a powerful woman, part lover and part muse, praising her strength and appetite for life. Around her he gathers striking images and hints of his own wish to return to work and public life after years away. The song charges forward with a hard, rolling groove and an urgent vocal. The Band plays tightly behind him, with Garth Hudson's organ and Robertson's guitar giving it a rough, exciting edge.
hazel: The singer is drawn to Hazel and describes her in admiring terms while confessing how much he needs her. It is a simple song of yearning, without a story or conflict beyond his desire and hope. The tone is warm and slightly melancholy, and the melody rises and falls gently. The Band supply a soft, rootsy backing that keeps it intimate and unhurried.
something-there-is-about-you: The singer tries to explain what it is about a particular woman that moves him so deeply. She seems to awaken his earliest memories, taking him back to his childhood in the north, and he concludes that he is devoted to her. The song mixes nostalgia and romance in a mood that is both tender and restless. Musically it rolls along at a steady mid-tempo, with The Band's organ and guitar weaving around the vocal.
dirge: The singer turns on himself, confessing shame for having needed someone or something that brought him only misery. He describes the relationship with a harsh, unforgiving clarity and insists he is done with it. The mood is dark and unrelenting, as the title suggests, with no consoling chorus. Dylan's heavy piano and voice are joined only by Robertson's acoustic guitar, which makes it one of the barest, most intense recordings in his catalogue.
you-angel-you: The singer simply celebrates the woman he loves, describing how completely she has captivated him. It is a light, happy song with no darker turn, built on a bright refrain that addresses her directly. The tone is playful and easygoing compared with the heavier songs elsewhere on the album. The Band give it a bouncy, rolling arrangement, with organ and guitar keeping it buoyant.
never-say-goodbye: The singer looks out on a cold, still winter landscape and turns to the woman he loves, wishing their time together would last. He dreams of the future and asks that there be no parting between them. The song is gentle and wistful, mixing quiet natural imagery with a simple plea. The Band's backing is soft and restrained, letting the mood of hushed affection come through.
youre-a-big-girl-now: A man speaks to a former lover who has grown independent and found a life without him. He admits how much the separation hurts and hints that he could become a different man if she would let him. The song moves in long, aching lines, his voice climbing high on each confession, more pleading than bitter. The Minneapolis band gives it a soft, rolling setting of acoustic guitars and organ.
meet-me-in-the-morning: A man calls out to a woman, asking her to meet him in the morning so the two of them can get away. He has been waiting and struggling for a long time, and his images of cold nights and dawn carry more doubt than hope. It is the plainest song on the album, a straight blues sung in a tired, patient voice. Electric guitar answers each line, giving it a smoky, late-night feel.
if-you-see-her-say-hello: A man speaks to someone who may run into his former lover, now far away, and asks them to give her his regards. He insists he bears no grudge and respects her choice, yet every message he sends reveals how much he still thinks about her. The song is gentle and controlled on the surface, the hurt showing only at the edges. A quiet acoustic arrangement with mandolin gives it a sad, tender glow.
odds-and-ends: A man complains about a lover who keeps letting things spill and slip, leaving him with nothing but scraps and loose ends. He sounds more exasperated than heartbroken, and by the end he is ready to walk away. The song is brief and breezy, built on a driving rock and roll beat with a shouted chorus. It sets the loose, good-humoured tone of the whole collection.
orange-juice-blues-blues-for-breakfast: This is the Band's track rather than Dylan's: a slow morning blues about a man left alone with his thoughts. He sits through breakfast feeling sorry for himself, missing someone and unable to shake the gloom. The song unfolds at an easy, sorrowful pace, its mood lifted only slightly by wry humour. Its soulful vocal and warm horns sound closer to rhythm and blues than to the rest of the basement recordings.
million-dollar-bash: The song gathers a cast of strange, comic characters who are all on their way to a big celebration. Each verse adds another absurd figure or mishap, and the chorus keeps returning to the promise of the party itself. It is pure fun, loose and laughing, with the feel of friends playing in a room for each other. The bouncing rhythm and group singing make it one of the most cheerful tracks on the album.
yazoo-street-scandal: This is one of the Band's own numbers: a rocking story about a seductive woman and the gossip that surrounds her on a notorious stretch of street. The singer is pulled in despite warnings, half thrilled and half afraid. The song moves fast, with a swampy Southern feel and a hard-driving beat. It shows the Band's taste for Southern settings and colourful, slightly lurid storytelling.
goin-to-acapulco: A man describes going down to Acapulco to spend time with a woman he knows there, as he does whenever life gets heavy. The words talk of good times, but the music is slow and weary, and his voice sounds resigned, almost grieving. That gap between what he says and how he sounds gives the song its strange power. The Band's organ and steady drums wrap it in a heavy, hymn-like mood.
katies-been-gone: This is a Band track, not a Dylan performance: a gentle lament from a man whose love has gone away. He waits and wonders whether she will come back, his loneliness growing with each verse. The song is soft and unhurried, with a tender, almost fragile vocal. Its quiet piano and organ give it the feel of a late-night ballad.
lo-and-behold: A man tells the story of a rambling journey from city to city, each stop bringing an odd encounter or a small comic misfortune. He moves on every time, never settling, and the chorus bursts in with a loud, exclaiming refrain. The song is playful and absurd, more a tall tale than a confession. The Band's rolling rhythm and harmony voices on the chorus make it feel like a group singalong.
bessie-smith: This is one of the Band's own songs, named for the classic blues singer Bessie Smith. The singer looks back on her and the vanished world she belonged to, searching for something of her that cannot be found again. The tone is warm and nostalgic rather than mournful. Its relaxed tempo and old-time feel suit its homage to an earlier era of American music.
clothes-line-saga: An ordinary household goes through the chore of bringing in the clothes from the line, and the narrator reports every small step. A neighbour mentions startling news from the wider world, but it gets the same shrug as the weather. The joke lies in the flat, matter-of-fact telling, which turns country life into gentle absurdity. The music is slow and plain, letting the storytelling carry the song.
apple-suckling-tree: The song is built like a children's rhyme, with a simple question-and-answer pattern and words chosen more for their sound than their sense. It hints at a meeting between two people under a tree, but any story is buried in silliness. Its charm is in its looseness, as if made up on the spot. A bouncing beat and a cheerful, rough-edged vocal keep it light from start to finish.
please-mrs-henry: A man who has had far too much to drink pleads with Mrs. Henry, who seems to run the place, to take pity on him. He is out of money, uncomfortable and fast losing his dignity, and each verse makes his plight sillier. The song is a broad comic turn, sung with a wobbly, mock-desperate swagger. The Band's slow, swaying accompaniment sounds like a tavern at closing time.
too-much-of-nothing: The song reflects on what happens when life holds too little: people grow mean, confused and cut off from one another. It reads like a dark proverb, moving through grim observations about history and human nature. A haunting refrain sends greetings to two absent women, adding a note of mystery. The slow, heavy beat and ghostly harmonies give it one of the most ominous moods on the album.
yea-heavy-and-a-bottle-of-bread: The song strings together odd, comic images of travel, food and getting ready to leave, without ever settling into a clear story. Its humour comes from how seriously it delivers pure nonsense, as if every detail mattered. The chorus repeats its strange title phrase like a slogan. The music lopes along at a lazy pace, loose and goofy, in the spirit of musicians amusing themselves.
aint-no-more-cane: This old work song comes from the convict labour camps of the American South, where prisoners were forced to cut sugar cane. It speaks of the harsh work, cruel overseers and the men who did not survive, along with the hope that such days will end. The Band's version passes the lead between several singers, giving it the feel of a shared lament. Acoustic instruments and rough harmonies keep it close to its folk roots.
crash-on-the-levee-down-in-the-flood: A man sees a flood coming and warns that the levee is about to give way. In the middle of the disaster, he tells the woman he is with that she will need to find someone else to lean on. The flood works as both a real danger and a picture of a relationship washing away. The song is a tough, rolling blues, delivered with grim good humour over a steady beat.
ruben-remus: This is one of the Band's own tracks, a lively song centred on a character named Ruben Remus. It has the loose, comic spirit of the basement sessions, telling its story with more energy than detail. The singers trade lines and lean into the fun of the tune. Its bouncing rhythm, piano and horns give it an old-fashioned, rollicking feel.
tiny-montgomery: The song announces the return of a mysterious figure called Tiny Montgomery and asks a string of strange, comic characters to spread the news. Each verse adds another nickname and another odd errand, building a crowded little world of rogues. It feels like a rumour passing through a small town. The music is loose and chugging, with a sly, half-spoken vocal.
dont-ya-tell-henry: This is the Band's performance of a Dylan song, a comic story of wandering, drinking and strange encounters. After each episode the singer insists that Henry must not hear about any of it, which becomes the running joke. The tone is boisterous and teasing, like a tall tale told in a bar. Horns and a stomping, good-time rhythm make it one of the album's liveliest tracks.
nothing-was-delivered: A man confronts someone who took something on trust and failed to deliver what was promised. He asks for an explanation and an admission, his tone patient but firm, as if the reckoning is overdue. The refrain sounds like a gentle farewell that is also a warning. The slow, rolling piano gives it the feel of an old rhythm and blues ballad.
open-the-door-homer: The song mixes a simple request to be let in with a string of cryptic sayings passed on from friends. Its advice touches on how to live, how to swim against the current and how to forgive, though it never quite explains itself. The refrain returns as a cheerful, insistent call at the door. The music is easygoing and warm, carried by the Band's relaxed groove and harmony vocals.
long-distance-operator: This is the Band's recording of a Dylan song: a blues in which a man begs the long distance operator to connect him. He is far from the woman he loves and growing frantic at every delay. The telephone becomes a picture of the distance between them. The Band gives it a heavy electric blues sound, with a raw, pleading vocal.
mozambique: The singer paints the African country of the title as an idyllic seaside place, a travel postcard where lovers meet by the water. It moves in short, lilting verses with no real story, simply luring the listener there with the promise of romance. Its easy tone stands out on an album otherwise full of long dramas and confessions. Scarlet Rivera's violin and Emmylou Harris's harmony give it a bright, swaying lift.
romance-in-durango: The narrator is a man on the run in Mexico, riding with his lover after shooting a man, and dreaming of the quiet life they will have once they reach safety. The song unfolds like a western film, with dust, heat, a fiesta and the constant sense of pursuit, until the ending turns dark and uncertain. Its chorus breaks into Spanish as he reassures her. The violin, accordion-like textures and harmonies give it a cinematic, border-town feel.
new-pony: The singer talks about a pony he once had and the new one that has replaced her, using the horse as a barely disguised image of desire and of a woman who has a hold on him. It is built on a slow, grinding blues riff, with the backing singers repeating a churchy call behind his lines. The mood is sexual and a little threatening, with hints of dark magic. Horns and the women's voices make it heavier than a plain twelve-bar blues.
no-time-to-think: The song is a long allegorical journey in which the narrator meets a parade of figures and ideas, from rulers and soldiers to a mysterious woman, each pulling him a different way. Verse after verse in a rolling three-time rhythm, it piles up grand abstractions while a refrain keeps returning to the pressure of having no space to think. The tone is weary and bewildered rather than angry. The violin and backing voices give it a stately, almost hypnotic sway.
baby-stop-crying: The singer speaks to a woman who is distraught after being hurt by someone else, and he offers himself as a friend and protector. Each verse sketches her trouble and his willingness to take her side, returning to a pleading chorus asking her to dry her tears. The tone is tender but also a little helpless, as if he is unsure she wants him. Slow, swelling saxophone and the backing singers give it a soulful, almost doo-wop warmth.
true-love-tends-to-forget: The narrator is in a relationship that leaves him weary and unsure, and he speaks to his lover about his doubts and his fear of being betrayed. The verses describe his exhaustion and restlessness, while the chorus turns his worry into a rueful observation about how love can be careless. The tone is wistful and pleading rather than bitter. The singers and horns give the song a smooth, almost pop sheen.
we-better-talk-this-over: The singer addresses a lover after things have gone wrong between them, proposing that they sit down and settle it before going separate ways. He moves between regret, wry humour and resignation, admitting his own confusion while insisting that staying together would only hurt them both. The song keeps a steady, upbeat pace that contrasts with its sad subject. It plays like a grown-up farewell rather than an angry one.
where-are-you-tonight-journey-through-da: The narrator travels through a shadowy landscape of strange figures and painful memories, all the while calling out to a woman who is gone. The verses tumble forward in crowded, symbolic images of struggle and temptation, until near the end he finds he has broken through his ordeal and is free of it, though still without her. The tone moves from anguish to a kind of fierce relief. The full band, horns and singers drive it with urgency.
do-right-to-me-baby-do-unto-others: The song works through a list of things the narrator will not do to other people, such as judging, cheating or hurting them, and pairs each with the hope that he will be spared the same. Its refrain returns to the Biblical rule of doing unto others as you would have them do unto you. The tone is calm and almost conversational, closer to a personal creed than a sermon. The smooth Muscle Shoals groove keeps it light and easy.
a-satisfied-mind: The song reflects on how people chase money and status, and how riches can vanish in a moment while a contented spirit lasts. It ends with the thought that the speaker will leave this life poor in goods but at peace. Dylan's version is brief and stately, sung close to the backing singers in a churchy, almost a cappella style. Placed first on Saved, it works like a quiet prayer before the louder gospel songs that follow.
covenant-woman: The narrator speaks with gratitude to a woman whom he sees as bound with him in a sacred promise, someone who understands him and has helped bring him closer to God. The verses mix personal tenderness with religious language, so that devotion to her and devotion to faith blur together. The tone is warm, humble and steady. A gentle keyboard-led arrangement keeps it intimate compared with the more fiery songs around it.
what-can-i-do-for-you: The song is a prayer addressed directly to God, in which the singer recounts how he has been rescued, guided and forgiven. Each verse adds to the list of gifts, and each time he returns to his humble question of what he could possibly give back. The tone is quiet, devotional and searching. Near the end a long, keening harmonica solo carries the feeling further than the words do.
in-the-garden: Starting with the arrest in the Garden of Gethsemane, the song moves through scenes from the Gospels, including miracles and the resurrection. After each scene it asks whether the witnesses understood what they were seeing, building a pattern of repeated questions. The tone is solemn and then increasingly triumphant. The arrangement climbs steadily, with chord changes rising and the backing singers swelling behind him to a powerful finish.
saving-grace: The narrator looks back on his life, considering the many times he might have died or gone astray, and credits his survival entirely to divine grace. Rather than preaching to others, he sounds grateful and almost surprised to be spared, and he looks ahead calmly to death. The tone is quiet, reverent and personal. The arrangement is spare and hymn-like, with organ and soft backing voices.
are-you-ready: The song is built almost entirely from questions put to the listener, and to the singer himself, about being ready for judgment, for the end of the world and for death. The backing singers echo and answer each question, giving it the feel of a church service. The tone is urgent and searching rather than condemning. Its driving rhythm and repeated refrain end Saved on a note of challenge.
heart-of-mine: The singer talks to his own heart as if it were a reckless friend, cautioning it to stay quiet and keep its distance from a woman it is drawn to. Each verse lists another warning, while the refrain keeps returning to this odd inner conversation. The tone is wry and self-mocking, as he clearly knows his heart may not listen. The relaxed, ragged band sound gives it a casual, late-night feel.
property-of-jesus: The song describes a man of faith who is laughed at, scorned and misunderstood by the people around him. Verse by verse the narrator turns on those mockers, listing their sneers and contrasting their shallow values with the believer's steadfastness. The tone is combative and scornful, closer to his old protest anger than to a hymn. A tough, driving band arrangement with backing singers gives it real bite.
watered-down-love: The song sets out a portrait of real love in the spirit of the famous passage from Corinthians, describing what it does and does not do. Against this ideal, the refrain dismisses the lesser, compromised love the world offers instead. The tone is cheerful and confident, more like a lesson than a confession. The breezy, almost pop arrangement keeps its moral message light on its feet.
the-grooms-still-waiting-at-the-altar: The narrator is looking for a woman who has disappeared, piecing together rumors of where she might be while the landscape around him grows violent and chaotic. Personal loss and visions of a world near collapse run together, so the song reads as both a love story and an apocalyptic warning. Its refrain returns to the image of a groom left waiting at a wedding. A fierce, driving rock arrangement makes it one of the most energetic tracks of the period.
dead-man-dead-man: The song addresses a dead man who stands for sin, pride and worldliness, and the narrator seems to be wrestling with that part of himself as much as with someone else. The verses describe the man's emptiness and the hold he has, while the refrain asks when he will come back to life. The tone is stern but restless. Its loose, swaying groove keeps the confrontation from becoming a sermon.
in-the-summertime: The narrator recalls a past summer when someone was close to him and he felt changed, and the song leaves open whether he means a woman, God or both. The verses drift between memory and the present, quietly weighing what was gained and what was lost. The tone is wistful and tender, with none of the album's sharper edges. Soft keyboards and harmonica give it a warm, unhurried glow.
trouble: The song is a catalogue of the world's troubles, moving from cities and politics to everyday life, each verse adding another place where misery and danger can be found. The refrain simply repeats the idea that there is trouble everywhere, with no solution offered. The tone is grim and matter-of-fact rather than preachy. It rides on a heavy, straightforward blues groove that suits its plain, relentless message.
man-of-peace: The song is a sermon in disguise, written soon after his gospel years: the devil, it argues, does not appear with horns but in the shape of a charming leader everyone wants to follow. Verse by verse it lists the many guises this figure can wear, and each one returns to the same unsettling refrain. The tone is dry and knowing rather than fiery. The band plays a long, swaying blues that keeps the warning sounding almost casual.
seeing-the-real-you-at-last: The singer looks back on a relationship in which he was taken in, and announces that the mask has finally slipped. Rather than grieving, he sounds wry and lightened, as though clear sight is its own reward. The verses are full of the tough-talking, film-noir attitude that runs through the album. The arrangement is punchy mid-1980s rock, with horns, backing singers and a bright, heavy drum sound.
ill-remember-you: The song is a farewell that refuses to be a goodbye: the singer admits that life will carry him on, but swears that this one person will stay with him. Its mood is grateful rather than bitter, looking back on what was shared instead of what went wrong. The melody is simple and rises gently into its title line. The recording is a mid-tempo ballad, warmer and less crowded than the rocking tracks around it.
clean-cut-kid: The song tells the story of a polite, wholesome young man who did everything his country asked and was sent to fight in Vietnam. On his return he is lost and violent, and the people around him cannot see how the nice boy they knew became this. Dylan tells it with bitter, black humour, piling up ironic details instead of preaching. The music is a fast, rowdy rock shuffle whose cheer sharpens the sting of the story.
never-gonna-be-the-same-again: The singer addresses a woman whose touch has left him altered, and he confesses it plainly, almost with gratitude. There is little story here; the song lingers on a single feeling of being shaken out of one's old self. Its tone is tender and slightly bashful, apologising and thanking at once. The recording leans on a gentle groove, keyboards and female backing vocals, making it one of the most polished, radio-minded sounds Dylan had attempted.
trust-yourself: The song is a sermon of self-reliance: the singer warns the listener not to hand their life over to someone else's promises or answers. Each verse names another kind of authority to be wary of, and each time the title phrase comes back as the remedy. Its tone is brisk and confident rather than angry. Musically it is built on a tight, funky groove with stabbing guitar and backing vocals answering the lead.
emotionally-yours: The song is a straightforward love letter, unusually unguarded for Dylan in this period. The singer pleads to be held and understood, and vows a devotion that does not depend on circumstances. It moves slowly, building to the title line at the close of each verse, with a feeling close to a classic pop standard. The recording is spare by the album's standards, carried by keyboards and a gentle rhythm under a tender vocal.
somethings-burning-baby: The singer speaks to a woman he can feel slipping away, convinced that a crisis is coming even though neither of them will name it. He presses her with questions, by turns suspicious and pleading, while the danger stays vague and smouldering. The mood is tense and foreboding, like a scene from a thriller. The music moves at a heavy, steady march, with a martial drum pattern and backing voices deepening the sense of threat.
you-wanna-ramble: The song is a jaunty rhythm and blues challenge from a man to a partner who cannot settle down. He lays down his terms with more swagger than heartbreak, half warning and half teasing. It moves on a simple, repeating structure built for dancing rather than storytelling. Dylan's version is a loose, upbeat band performance with backing singers, a light-hearted start to an album made largely of covers and collaborations.
precious-memories: The hymn is a meditation on remembrance: the singer finds that memories of parents, home and old worship come back to console him in later life. It is gentle and devotional, moving through short verses to a familiar chorus about those memories lingering. Dylan's recording sets the old church song to a swaying, island-style groove with backing singers, turning a solemn standard into something warm and easy-going. It is one of the few explicitly religious songs on the album.
maybe-someday: The singer addresses a woman who has left him, and runs through what might happen if she ever thinks better of it. The words tumble out quickly, mixing hurt pride, sarcasm and a lingering wish that she might come back. The title becomes a refrain that sounds less hopeful each time. The recording rushes along at a hectic tempo, with gospel-style backing voices and a busy band nearly overrunning the vocal.
got-my-mind-made-up: The singer announces that he is going, and the song is all momentum: his bags are packed, his reasons are settled, and the arguments for staying no longer reach him. The mood is restless and defiant, with flashes of humour rather than sorrow. It works like a classic leaving song, one verse of reasons after another. The recording is a tough, straight-ahead rock performance with the Heartbreakers, among the liveliest band tracks on the album.
under-your-spell: The singer speaks to a woman whose hold over him is almost supernatural, and the song wavers between surrender and resistance. He sounds bewitched and wary at once, promising to return even as he goes. The tone is wistful and slightly mysterious, ending the album on a quieter note than it began. The arrangement is a mid-tempo pop-rock ballad with backing singers and a smooth 1980s sheen.
lets-stick-together: The song is a plea to keep a marriage whole: the singer reminds his partner of the vows they made and argues that splitting up would hurt everyone, the children included. It is direct and good-humoured, more persuasion than lament, with a simple refrain that drives the point home. Dylan's recording is a rough, rocking rhythm and blues romp with harmonica, a loose and energetic start to an album built mostly from other people's songs.
when-did-you-leave-heaven: The song is a classic Tin Pan Alley compliment: the singer treats his beloved as an angel who has strayed to earth and asks, with mock seriousness, how heaven could have let her go. It is sweet, courtly and old-fashioned, built on a gentle melody and a single extended conceit. Dylan sings it softly over a sparse, keyboard-heavy backing, foreshadowing his much later albums of standards from the same era.
sally-sue-brown: The song is a breathless celebration of a girl the singer cannot get out of his head. He sings her praises and admits she has the upper hand, but he is too happy to mind. There is no real story, just infatuation sustained over a bouncing beat. Dylan's version is a ragged, fast rock and roll performance with loud guitars and backing vocals, sounding like a lively bar band rather than a polished studio take.
had-a-dream-about-you-baby: The song is a simple, rocking piece of desire: the singer has dreamed about a woman and wakes up preoccupied with her. He describes her with playful exaggeration and repeats the title as a hook rather than telling a story. The tone is lusty and fun, closer to vintage rock and roll than to his serious songwriting. The recording is a driving guitar rocker, short and loud, made to suit the film's rock-star setting.
ugliest-girl-in-the-world: The song is a comic love song turned upside down: instead of praising his sweetheart's looks, the singer happily lists how plain she is. The joke is that the more he runs her down, the clearer it becomes that he adores her. The tone is good-natured and silly, never cruel. The recording is a bouncy, uptempo rock and roll number that plays the novelty idea for laughs.
ninety-miles-an-hour-down-a-dead-end-str: The song pictures an illicit love affair as a car speeding toward a wall: both lovers can see the crash coming but neither will brake. The singer is resigned rather than defiant, admitting guilt and inevitability in the same breath. It is a classic country cheating song, built on a single strong image. Dylan's recording slows it right down, with a gentle band and harmony voices, giving it a mournful, almost gospel calm.
shenandoah: The song is one of the oldest and best-loved American folk tunes, a slow lament from someone travelling away from a beloved place and person, with the Shenandoah and Missouri rivers standing for home and distance. Its long, rolling melody gives it a sense of vast space. Dylan sings it with a full chorus of backing singers and a stately rhythm, ending an uneven album on a solemn, old-time note.
where-teardrops-fall: The singer speaks to a woman he loves, picturing a distant place where grief gathers and pledging to find her there. Around that promise he sets night images, passing time and an awareness that the world is unsettled. The tone is hushed and patient rather than pleading. Musically it is one of the gentlest moments on the album, a slow sway with saxophone and accordion drifting under his voice.
disease-of-conceit: Dylan treats conceit as a sickness spreading from person to person across the country, more dangerous than any physical plague. He describes what it does to people: it inflates them, isolates them and finally brings them down. The song moves like a stern moral lesson delivered with sorrow rather than anger. Its stately piano and sombre singing give it the feel of a hymn sung in a darkened church.
what-was-it-you-wanted: The whole song is a string of questions put to someone who has approached the singer, perhaps a lover, perhaps a fan or a hanger-on. He wonders what they came for, whether he has already given it and whether he heard them right. The repeated questioning turns wary and faintly mocking, with a sense that the relationship is a game neither side admits to. The sound is swampy and hazy, typical of the album's night-time atmosphere.
unbelievable: The singer looks around at a society that seems to run on money, deceit and empty promises, and keeps declaring how hard it is to believe. Each verse adds another absurdity, delivered with a shrug as much as a protest. The refrain turns disbelief into a running joke. The band plays a bright, driving rock arrangement that sits in wry contrast to the bleak picture the words paint.
t-v-talkin-song: The narrator wanders into a park where a street preacher is warning a crowd about the evils of television and what it does to families and minds. As the speech goes on, the audience grows restless and a riot breaks out. In a closing twist, the narrator later watches the whole commotion broadcast on TV. Told with deadpan humour, it is both a satire of media and a gentle mockery of the preacher himself.
10-000-men: The song paints a procession of ten thousand men, sometimes soldiers on a hill, sometimes figures in an odd dream, each verse adding a new detail in the manner of a counting rhyme. Between these images the singer turns to address a woman at home. The effect is playful and ominous at once, like a children's chant with something dark underneath. The band settles into a heavy, unhurried blues groove.
2-x-2: Built like a children's counting game, the song lines figures up two by two, three by three and onward, recalling the animals entering the ark. As the numbers climb, the questions it asks grow more uneasy: where are they all going, and what is waiting for them. The simple structure carries a sense of judgment and passing time. It moves at a gentle, rolling pace with a soft, repeating melody.
god-knows: Addressed partly to a lover and partly to the world, the song rests on the idea that God understands what people cannot say or fix themselves. It acknowledges hardship, separation and a world that may end, yet holds to a steady trust. Each verse returns to that refrain of divine knowledge. The recording starts sparse and gathers force, ending in a rousing, rock-driven finish.
handy-dandy: The song circles a figure called Handy Dandy, a carefree ladies' man who seems to have everything and to owe nothing to anyone. Scenes of parties, women and idle talk pass by as the narrator watches him with amusement and a hint of judgment. The name itself, taken from an old children's guessing game, suggests a trickster. The band plays a loose, jaunty groove dominated by a bright organ.
cats-in-the-well: Taking its title from an old children's rhyme, the song pictures a world in which danger is close and nobody is coming to help. Images of decline pile up, from neglected homes to an approaching sense of doom, delivered with a calm, almost matter-of-fact voice. It closes with a plea for mercy from above, turning the song into a prayer. The band drives it as a tough, rocking shuffle.
jim-jones: Jim Jones is a prisoner shipped from England to the penal colony at Botany Bay. The song follows his voyage and his harsh treatment, and ends with his resolve to escape, join the outlaws in the bush and turn on those who held him. It is a song of defiance more than despair. Dylan sings it alone with acoustic guitar, in a measured, weathered voice that suits the old story.
blackjack-davey: The ballad tells of a charming traveller who sings at a lady's door and wins her over. She leaves her comfortable house, her husband and her fine clothes to go with him, and when her husband rides after her she refuses to come back. It celebrates choosing freedom and passion over wealth and duty. Dylan performs it solo with a steady, rolling guitar pattern.
canadee-i-o: A girl dresses as a sailor so she can board a ship bound for Canada. When the crew discovers she is a woman they turn against her, but the captain protects her, and by the end she has married him and settled in the new land. It is a tale of courage and luck told in a long, flowing narrative. Dylan sings it gently over a delicate, ringing guitar part.
sittin-on-top-of-the-world: The singer has been abandoned by a lover who went away and did not come back. Rather than mourn, he claims to be doing better than ever, though the boast carries a clear trace of hurt. The song is built on a simple, repeated refrain that turns heartbreak into stubborn pride. Dylan plays it as a relaxed country blues with guitar and harmonica, an old standard handed down through many singers.
little-maggie: The singer describes Maggie, a lively and reckless woman he cannot stop loving even as she spends her time drinking and going with other men. He turns between admiration, jealousy and resignation, and thinks of leaving. The song is short and quick, built on a driving rhythm taken from mountain music. Dylan delivers it in a rough, urgent voice over fast strummed guitar.
hard-times: The song asks listeners to pause amid their own comfort and remember those who are hungry, weary and poor. Its refrain is a quiet wish that hardship would leave and not return, sung on behalf of everyone who suffers. Written as a gentle, hymn-like piece, it has outlasted its century as a standard of compassion. Dylan sings it slowly and plainly with acoustic guitar, letting its sorrow carry it.
step-it-up-and-go: This is a jaunty, ragtime-flavoured blues made of short, comic verses about people and their foibles, each one capped by the title as a refrain. There is little story; the fun lies in the rhythm and the wit. Dylan plays it fast with a bouncing fingerpicked guitar, singing with obvious enjoyment, a brief burst of energy among the album's darker ballads.
tomorrow-night: The singer is with someone he loves and is happy tonight, but he cannot stop worrying about tomorrow and whether her feelings will last. The song is a soft, romantic pop ballad from before the rock and roll era, built on that single fear. Dylan gives it a crooning, intimate reading with just his guitar, an early sign of his later love for old popular standards.
youre-gonna-quit-me: The singer can tell that his partner is preparing to walk away, and he pleads, half resigned and half hopeful, for her to stay. The song turns on that single fear, returning to it again and again in the manner of a classic blues. It is short and spare. Dylan plays it with a nimble fingerpicked guitar and sings it with a worn, close-up intimacy.
diamond-joe: The narrator has signed on to work for a man named Diamond Joe, and soon regrets it: the food is poor, the pay is meagre and the work is hard. He tells his story with a wry, weary humour, warning others not to make his mistake and dreaming of escape. It is an old western work song of grievance. Dylan sings it solo in a rugged voice over a steady strum.
love-henry: An old ballad of love turned to murder: a man arrives to tell a woman he loves someone else, and she kills him and hides his body. A talking bird has seen everything and refuses to keep her secret. Dylan sings it slowly and flatly, letting the cold facts carry the horror. It is just his worn voice and a single acoustic guitar.
ragged-and-dirty: A plain-spoken blues from a man who has been thrown out and is broke, shabby and alone, pleading with a woman to let him back in. The verses circle around the same situation rather than telling a story, in the way of old country blues. Dylan plays it with a loose, rolling guitar pattern and sings with a rough, unhurried patience.
blood-in-my-eyes: A blues about longing: a man is so taken with a woman that he can think of nothing else, and he offers what little he has to win her over. It repeats its situation like a lament rather than moving forward, and its mood is weary more than lustful. Dylan slows the original's string-band lilt into a dark, deliberate solo performance on acoustic guitar.
broke-down-engine: A man left by his lover describes himself as a broken-down machine, out of power and useless without her. He prays and pleads for her to come back, his bad luck piling up as he goes. Dylan's version is fierce and percussive, with hard-strummed guitar and a hoarse vocal that turns McTell's lament into something close to a shout.
two-soldiers: A ballad about two soldiers before a battle: one has family waiting at home, the other has no one who will miss him. They make promises to one another about who will carry word home, and then the fighting takes them both. Dylan sings it gently and without drama, letting the quiet telling make the loss feel heavier.
jack-a-roe: A ballad about a rich young woman whose sweetheart is sent off to war against her parents' wishes. She dresses as a man, enlists under a false name and goes after him, finding him wounded on the battlefield and nursing him back to health before they marry. Dylan tells the story briskly and plainly, sounding like a storyteller passing on something old.
lone-pilgrim: A hymn in which a visitor stands at the grave of a stranger who died while journeying, and the dead pilgrim answers, telling him not to grieve because he is at rest and at home. It turns a lonely death into a calm acceptance. Dylan sings it quietly and tenderly, a soft ending to an album full of murder and misfortune.
dirt-road-blues: A man on foot along a country road keeps moving, waiting for a woman to come back and wondering if she ever will. The song is short and repetitive, more a mood than a story, with the road standing in for a restless, unsettled mind. Its sound is lo-fi and echoing, a bouncing old-time rhythm under Dylan's distant, roughened voice.
million-miles: A man speaks to a woman who seems impossibly distant from him, though he keeps telling himself he is getting nearer. The song drifts through scraps of thought, regret and wry asides, its refrain measuring the gap between them. The band plays a low, loping groove with organ and guitar, and Dylan's voice sounds tired and sly at once.
til-i-fell-in-love-with-you: A man describes how falling in love has left him worn out and damaged, unable to rest or think clearly, with his life falling apart around him. Each verse adds another sign of his decline, and the refrain blames it all on love. The tone is grim but wryly funny, set over a grinding blues groove with a thick, murky sound.
cant-wait: A man tormented by desire tells a woman that he is running out of patience and running out of time, haunted by thoughts of her day and night. The song moves with a heavy, dragging gait, its refrain pressing the same urgency again and again. Organ and a dark, rumbling band surround Dylan's weathered voice, giving it the feel of a late-night confession.
bye-and-bye: A man courts a woman with a relaxed, sweet-talking manner, saying he is in no hurry and enjoying himself. But beneath the charm the singer drops darker hints about his past and his intentions, so the courtship never feels quite innocent. Dylan croons it softly over a lilting swing arrangement that recalls the popular ballads of the 1930s.
lonesome-day-blues: A man having a dreadful, lonely day pours out a string of grievances, losses and boasts, moving from family memories to threats against his enemies. The verses pile up loosely, as in old blues, mixing sorrow, humor and menace.
