A tough, relentless band groove pushes it along, and Dylan sings in a gravelly growl that keeps the mood both mournful and defiant.
floater-too-much-to-ask: An older narrator muses about his family, his youth, a romance and the passing of time, wandering from topic to topic like a man fishing on a lazy afternoon. His wit is dry and sometimes unsettling, with flashes of violence under the calm. The music is a lilting, old-fashioned swing with fiddle, giving the song the easy feel of a porch tune.
moonlight: A man speaks tenderly to a woman, asking her to meet him in the evening and painting a lush, romantic picture of nature at dusk. Each verse returns to the same invitation, so the song feels like a patient serenade. Dylan sings it in a light, crooning style over a lilting arrangement, sounding like a parlour song from long before rock and roll.
cry-a-while: A man who was hurt in love turns the tables, telling the woman who treated him badly that now she will be the one crying. The verses are full of sardonic asides and tough talk. The song alternates between a slow, menacing blues and sudden bursts of a fast shuffle, giving it a lurching, unpredictable energy.
beyond-the-horizon: A man speaks to someone he loves, assuring them that something better lies past the horizon, beyond the world's troubles. The song is a gentle reverie, blending romance with a quiet sense of faith in what lies ahead. Its arrangement is soft and swaying, like an old dance-band ballad, and Dylan sings it with an unexpected tenderness.
nettie-moore: A man longs for a woman named Nettie Moore, who seems lost to him, while describing a world full of danger, hardship and approaching judgment. The verses roam between grief, scripture, blues images and wry asides before returning to the sorrowful refrain. The arrangement is sparse and stately, built on a slow, thudding beat, with Dylan sounding grave and reflective.
the-levees-gonna-break: A man watches as the river rises and warns that the levee is about to fail, the coming flood standing for both natural disaster and a life spinning out of control. Released the year after Hurricane Katrina, it inevitably recalled that flood. The verses toss together worry, love and sardonic remarks over a fast, rolling boogie driven by the road band.
do-you-hear-what-i-hear: The song is a chain of messages: each figure hears or sees something and passes it on to the next, from the smallest creature up to a mighty ruler. It grows step by step, each verse a little grander, until the closing call is for peace and goodness for all. Dylan takes it straight and earnest, his rough voice set against a warm, old-fashioned arrangement with backing singers.
winter-wonderland: The song follows two sweethearts out in the snow, delighting in sleigh bells, a snowman and the cold that sends them back by the fire. It is less about Christmas itself than about winter romance, and its mood is light and playful throughout. Dylan gives it a brisk, cheerful swing with a chorus of backing voices, and his gravelly delivery makes its innocence sound both sincere and a little comic.
hark-the-herald-angels-sing: This is a hymn of proclamation: the angels' message of a newborn king is relayed to the world, and the listener is asked to join in. Its verses move from the birth itself to what it means for believers, ending in joyful praise. Dylan sings it plainly and reverently, letting the choir carry much of the melody, and makes no attempt to dress up a song meant for a congregation.
ill-be-home-for-christmas: The singer is writing home, perhaps a soldier, asking for snow, mistletoe and presents to be ready for a homecoming. Only at the end does the twist arrive: the reunion may happen only in dreams. The song is short and gentle, its warmth shadowed by distance. Dylan sings it slowly and tenderly, and his worn voice brings out the longing beneath its holiday cheer.
little-drummer-boy: The song tells of a boy summoned to see the infant Jesus who has no fine present to bring, so he plays his drum for the child instead. Its refrain imitates the beat of the drum, and the story ends with the baby smiling at him. The point is humility: the gift that matters is the one honestly given. Dylan's version keeps a steady marching beat and a soft choir behind his voice.
o-come-all-ye-faithful-adeste-fideles: The hymn is an invitation: believers are called to travel to Bethlehem and adore the child born there. Each verse repeats the call, building to a rousing refrain of worship. Dylan opens in Latin, a nod to the song's origins, then carries on in English with a choir behind him. His grainy, unpolished voice against the stately hymn tune gives the track an unusual, heartfelt character.
have-yourself-a-merry-little-christmas: The singer comforts someone, hoping the coming holiday brings relief from the year's worries and a return of old friends. Beneath its warmth lies a quiet sadness: the good times are hoped for rather than promised. The song moves slowly and tenderly, a lullaby more than a celebration. Dylan croons it gently over a soft, old-fashioned band arrangement, sounding both tender and weathered.
silver-bells: The song paints a crowded city at holiday time: sidewalks full of people, shop windows lit, children laughing and bells ringing on every corner. It is a picture of urban bustle turned festive, with a gentle refrain about the bells. Dylan sings it in an easy, swaying style with backing singers, treating it as an affectionate snapshot of an old-time American Christmas.
the-first-noel: The carol retells the Nativity story: angels appear to shepherds in the fields, a star rises in the east, and wise men travel to bring gifts to the child. Each verse ends with the same joyful refrain. It is calm and narrative, less a celebration than a recounting. Dylan's version leans on its choir, his voice blending into a slow, reverent arrangement.
christmas-island: This is a playful daydream: rather than a snowy holiday, the singer imagines Christmas on a warm island, with Santa arriving by canoe and the season spent under the palms. The tone is breezy and romantic, closer to a holiday postcard than a carol. Dylan gives it a relaxed, swaying feel with a Hawaiian-style lilt, one of the album's lightest moments.
the-christmas-song: The song is a string of cozy images: roasting chestnuts, carols, decorations and children waiting for Santa, rounded off with a wish that everyone has a good holiday. It is unhurried and intimate, more a mood than a story. Dylan sings it slowly over a soft jazz-tinged arrangement, and his cracked voice gives a song associated with velvet crooners a more fragile, human sound.
o-little-town-of-bethlehem: The hymn looks on Bethlehem at night, still and silent, as the birth of Christ takes place unnoticed by the world. Later verses turn the scene into a prayer that the same presence might be born in the believer's heart. It is hushed and contemplative throughout. Dylan sings it simply with a choir, ending the album in reverence rather than celebration.
my-wifes-home-town: The singer complains about the place his wife comes from, blaming it for everything that goes wrong and casting it as something close to hell. The humor is dark and deadpan, a classic blues grievance played for laughs and menace at once. It moves on a slow, heavy Chicago blues riff, with accordion and growling guitar, and Dylan delivers it with a gruff, sly relish.
if-you-ever-go-to-houston: The singer speaks as someone who has been around Texas, handing out tips on how to carry yourself in Houston and asking to be remembered to people there. Between the advice come hints of an old love and unfinished business. It rolls along at an easy, swinging pace, and the accordion gives it the feel of a Tex-Mex dance hall, with Dylan sounding wry and worn.
forgetful-heart: The singer addresses his heart directly, as if it were a companion that has drifted off and lost the memory of a past love. He is left behind, lonely and sleepless, while the love fades into the past. The song is brooding and spare, built on a slow, haunting groove with mournful accordion and violin, and Dylan sings it in a low, ghostly voice.
jolene: The singer is a confident rambler who names his woman as his queen and himself as king, mixing devotion with bravado. The repeated name serves as the song's hook, coming back after every short verse. It is loose and rough, a road-house shuffle with crunching guitar and accordion, and Dylan sings it with a grin in his voice.
this-dream-of-you: The singer is alone, uncertain and tired of the world, and what holds him up is a vision of someone he loves, whether real or only remembered. He fears what will happen if the dream fades. The song sways gently like a border waltz, with accordion and fiddle carrying a sweet, melancholy tune, and Dylan sings it with weary tenderness.
shake-shake-mama: The song is a party blues: the singer calls on a woman to move, while slipping in boasts and complaints about his own hard situation. Its verses are short and punchy, each returning to the title cry. The music is a rough, driving shuffle with stinging guitar and accordion, and Dylan growls through it in the spirit of old Chicago and Memphis records.
its-all-good: The song surveys a world going wrong, marriages failing, the powerful lying, towns falling apart, and answers each bad sign with the same breezy reassurance of its title. The gap between the grim pictures and the upbeat refrain is the joke, and the bite. It bounces along on a bright, swinging groove with accordion, and Dylan sounds amused and knowing.
soon-after-midnight: A man awake in the small hours waits for a woman and tells her how devoted he is. The song moves at an easy, swaying pace, sweet on the surface, but darker hints of jealousy and violence surface between the romantic lines, so the tenderness never feels entirely safe. The band plays softly behind a croon that is half lullaby, half warning, which makes it one of the gentlest and strangest moments on a dark record.
narrow-way: A narrator who has wandered and suffered addresses a woman who keeps her distance, swearing that if he cannot climb up to her, she will one day have to come down to him. Verse after verse returns to that promise as a refrain, mixing boasts, grievances and stray images of hardship and travel. The groove barely changes, rolling forward relentlessly, and the song's length turns it into an endurance test of longing and pride.
long-and-wasted-years: Addressed to someone the narrator once loved, the song looks back over a broken relationship and the time both of them squandered. Its tone is regretful but also defensive and bitter, moving between apology, accusation and resignation without settling. The verses are short and conversational, almost like a man thinking aloud. A repeating guitar pattern carries it forward steadily, and Dylan's growled delivery makes the regret sound lived-in rather than sentimental.
pay-in-blood: The speaker is a hard, menacing figure who seems to have seen corruption and cruelty everywhere and answers it with threats of his own. Each verse piles up insults, boasts and grim pronouncements, and the refrain returns to the idea that his payment comes in blood. The music is jaunty and polished, which makes the venom in the vocal even more unsettling. It is one of the angriest songs on an already violent album.
scarlet-town: The song describes a strange town drawn from old folk balladry, a place full of mourners, sinners, beauty and ruin. Rather than tell a single story, it moves from scene to scene, sketching characters and images in a slow, hypnotic procession. The mood is mournful and eerie, like a ghost story set to a dirge. Banjo and fiddle give it an old-time sound, as if a centuries-old ballad has been reopened and filled with new shadows.
early-roman-kings: The song describes a gang of arrogant, well-dressed strongmen, part ancient emperors and part modern hoodlums, and the narrator sometimes seems to speak as one of them. It unfolds as a series of boasts and threats over a single stomping riff that never lets up. The tone is darkly comic and menacing at once. An accordion adds a dusty, border-town color to the grinding Chicago-style blues underneath.
tin-angel: A man comes home to find his wife has left with another man, and he sets out after them. The song tells the story in many verses like an old murder ballad, with dialogue between the three characters as the chase reaches its violent end. There is no chorus, just the steady unfolding of the plot over a dark, repetitive acoustic groove. Its tone is fatalistic, as if the tragedy were written long before it began.
the-night-we-called-it-a-day: The singer recalls the evening a love affair came to an end, when even nature seemed to share in the sorrow. It is a classic torch song, quiet and wistful, dwelling on a single remembered moment rather than telling a long story. Dylan sings it slowly and plainly, without the polish of a crooner, and his small band plays softly with pedal steel guitar standing in for the lush strings of the original arrangements.
stay-with-me: Unlike most songs on the album, this one is addressed to God rather than to a lover. The singer confesses to feeling lost and unworthy and asks for a guiding presence to stay close. It moves slowly and solemnly, like a hymn, with no real refrain beyond its repeated plea. Dylan's recording is hushed and spare, his voice exposed and fragile over a soft, sparse band.
autumn-leaves: The singer watches the leaves drift past a window and is reminded of a lover who has left, and of the summer they shared. It is a short, simple song built on the image of the changing season as a measure of passing time and fading love. Dylan sings it very slowly and quietly, letting the melody carry the sadness, while the band keeps to a soft, sparse accompaniment.
why-try-to-change-me-now: The singer admits he has always been a bit odd and out of step, and asks his lover why she would want to change him after all this time. The song has a gentle, self-mocking humor and a tone of quiet pleading. It moves easily through its verses without a big climax. Dylan's plain, weathered voice suits the idea of a man set in his ways, and the band's soft, slow arrangement keeps it intimate.
some-enchanted-evening: The singer describes seeing a stranger across a crowded room and knowing at once that this is the person meant for you. The song urges the listener to act on that feeling before it slips away. In the musical it is a grand, operatic showpiece, but Dylan's version strips it down to a slow, almost conversational reading, with steel guitar and quiet bass, making it sound more like a private memory than a declaration.
where-are-you: The singer is left alone after a lover's departure and keeps asking where that person has gone and what became of the promises they shared. It is a pure lament, built on repeated questions that get no answers. The mood is lonely and still. Dylan sings it slowly and tenderly over a hushed arrangement, letting long pauses and the drifting pedal steel fill the empty space the song describes.
what-ill-do: The singer has lost someone and can only imagine the empty days ahead, filled with memories and photographs instead of company. The song is a waltz built around a series of quiet, helpless questions. Its tone is tender and resigned rather than dramatic. Dylan's version is slow and unadorned, with the band barely above a whisper, so the old melody and his worn voice carry all the feeling.
maybe-youll-be-there: The singer is alone, looking back on a love that slipped away and imagining that one day, somewhere, that person may turn up again. It is a quiet torch song where hope and doubt are mixed in equal measure. The melody rises gently and falls back without resolving. Dylan sings it softly with his touring band, keeping the arrangement light and unhurried so the wistful mood can settle.
polka-dots-and-moonbeams: The song tells a small, storybook romance: a chance meeting at a dance, an instant attraction, and a happy future that follows. Its images are whimsical and gentle, and its tone is warm and a little nostalgic. Unlike many of the sad ballads on these standards albums, it is light and charming. Dylan's band plays it at an easy, swaying tempo, and his voice treats it fondly, like a memory of a simpler time.
skylark: The singer speaks to a bird in flight, asking it to carry news of a love that might be waiting in some faraway place. The song is full of yearning and imagery of open skies, distant meadows and night. Its long, winding melody is famously demanding to sing. Dylan takes it slowly and carefully, his band playing a soft, airy backing that leaves room for the melody's wandering phrases.
nevertheless: The singer knows that this romance could bring heartbreak and that friends would advise caution, yet admits to being hopelessly in love regardless. The song is light and good-humored, more amused than anguished about its own foolishness. It moves at an easy, strolling pace. Dylan's version is relaxed and affectionate, with the band's gentle swing and steel guitar giving it a soft, slightly old-fashioned glow.
all-or-nothing-at-all: The singer lays down terms to a would-be partner, insisting that a half-hearted love is worse than none and that only total commitment will do. Beneath the demand is a fear of being hurt, which gives the song its tension. The melody builds with a slow, insistent pulse. Dylan's band plays it with a darker, Latin-tinged rhythm than most of the album, and his delivery is firm rather than pleading.
on-a-little-street-in-singapore: The singer describes a clandestine love affair set on a quiet street in a distant Asian port, with moonlight, exotic surroundings and a sense of danger. It is a piece of old Hollywood-style romantic escapism, more about atmosphere than story. The tune sways lazily, evoking a faraway night. Dylan's version is gentle and unhurried, his band adding a soft, slightly mysterious color that suits the song's dreamlike setting.
it-had-to-be-you: The singer explains that many others might have seemed better suited, yet none could hold their interest the way this one person does, even with all their faults. It is affectionate and lightly teasing, a song of contented love rather than longing. The melody is bouncy and familiar. Dylan's band gives it a relaxed, easy swing, and his voice treats the old standard with an unforced warmth.
that-old-black-magic: The singer describes love as a kind of sorcery that sets them spinning and burning whenever their lover is near. The song piles up images of enchantment, fire and helpless surrender, and its long, climbing melody mirrors the feeling of being swept away. It is one of the most upbeat songs on the album. Dylan's band plays it with a brisk, loping swing, giving the record a lively change of pace.
come-rain-or-come-shine: The singer vows steady devotion through good times and bad, rich or poor, happy or troubled. It is a vow song, calm and certain rather than anxious, built on a simple contrast between fair and foul weather. Placed at the end of the album, it closes the record on a note of commitment. Dylan sings it slowly and earnestly, with his band's soft, warm backing giving the promise a sense of quiet dignity.
i-guess-ill-have-to-change-my-plans: A man discovers that the person he was building his life around has moved on, and he takes the news with a rueful shrug rather than a scene. The song is light on its feet, turning heartbreak into a wry admission that the plans have to change. Dylan sings it with a relaxed, conversational phrasing over his touring band, setting the easygoing, late-night tone for the three discs that follow.
i-could-have-told-you: The singer looks back on a love that ended the way he always suspected it would, and he speaks with more weariness than bitterness. The song is a slow, brooding ballad, built on the gap between knowing and still being unable to stop yourself. Dylan takes it at a patient pace with a muted band, letting his weathered voice carry the sense of someone who learned nothing from his own warnings.
once-upon-a-time: An older narrator recalls a time when he was young, in love and sure the world was his, and sets it against the quieter present. The song moves like a fairy tale turned inside out, its gentle opening giving way to the sadness of things that did not last. Dylan sings it slowly and tenderly, and his aged voice gives the memory of youth a real distance.
this-nearly-was-mine: Written for a character who believes he has lost the woman he loves, the song is a lament for something that was close enough to touch and is now out of reach. It is a sweeping waltz in its stage form, full of grand longing. Dylan pares it down, with pedal steel and brushed rhythm under his voice, so the regret sounds private and late rather than operatic.
that-old-feeling: The singer runs into someone he once loved and realises his feelings never went away, however much time has passed. The song is bright and swinging rather than mournful, treating the rekindled spark as both a surprise and a small helplessness. Dylan's version moves at an easy mid-tempo, with his band giving it a loose, small-combo bounce among the slower ballads around it.
it-gets-lonely-early: The song is about the empty hours after a relationship ends, when the night seems to arrive early and there is no one to share it with. It is a quiet, reflective ballad about ageing and solitude rather than fresh heartbreak. Dylan sings it gently over a spare arrangement, and the slow tempo lets the loneliness settle in rather than being declared.
my-one-and-only-love: This is a straightforward love song, addressed directly to one person and full of quiet wonder at what she means to the singer. It unfolds slowly, more a hushed confession than a declaration. Dylan treats it with restraint, his voice low and close over soft steel guitar and bass, making it one of the most tender moments on the first disc.
trade-winds: Set somewhere in the islands, the song has the singer listening to the winds off the sea and thinking of a romance that once happened there. It is dreamy and exotic in the manner of its era, with a gentle sway that suggests palms and water. Dylan's band gives it a soft, drifting arrangement with steel guitar, ending the first disc on a wistful, faraway note.
braggin: The song is a light, teasing piece in which the singer cannot stop showing off about the person he loves. It is one of the more upbeat tracks on the album, built on a bouncing swing rhythm and a sense of humour about its own boasting. Dylan sounds amused and relaxed, and the band keeps the groove brisk, a cheerful start to a disc that soon turns darker.
imagination: The song considers how the mind dresses up love, conjuring a perfect partner and making a person believe what they want to believe. It moves between wonder and gentle doubt, never quite settling which one wins. Dylan sings it as a slow, thoughtful ballad, his phrasing unhurried, with the band sketching a soft late-night backdrop behind him.
how-deep-is-the-ocean: The whole song is built on a series of questions about the size of the singer's love, each answered with an image from nature that has no measurable end. It is simple and devotional, a pledge made through comparisons rather than promises. Dylan takes it slowly and plainly, letting the questions hang in the air over a hushed band.
p-s-i-love-you: The song takes the form of a letter from someone separated from his partner, passing on everyday details about how he is getting on before coming to the real point at the end. Its charm lies in that homely, chatty tone, with the feeling held back until the closing line. Dylan delivers it like someone reading his own note aloud, warm and slightly shy, over a gentle arrangement.
the-best-is-yet-to-come: The singer is wooing someone and assures them that everything so far is merely a warm-up for what is coming. It is a confident, swaggering song, full of anticipation and a little flirtation. Dylan's version swings at a steady, unhurried pace, and his older voice gives the promise an amused, knowing edge that a young singer could not bring to it.
but-beautiful: The song tries to pin down what love is and keeps finding contradictions: it can be one thing and its opposite in the same moment. It is a reflective ballad more than a personal story, a meditation in the form of a love song. Dylan sings it softly, almost musing to himself, with spare guitar and steel shading the melody.
heres-that-rainy-day: The singer looks back at a carefree past when love seemed endless and any thought of trouble could be brushed aside, then admits that the day he never planned for has come. It is a sorrowful ballad about the cost of not saving anything for later, emotionally speaking. Dylan's slow, rueful reading suits a song about hindsight, and his band keeps the arrangement grey and still.
where-is-the-one: The song is a search with no answer: the singer wonders aloud where his true love might be and why she has not appeared. It is a melancholy, searching ballad with an unusual, winding melody. Dylan sings it with quiet resignation over a subdued arrangement, letting the unanswered question stand at the centre of a disc full of lonely late-night songs.
theres-a-flaw-in-my-flue: The song mixes comedy and heartbreak: the singer sits by a faulty fireplace, and every time it smokes and sputters he is reminded of the person he has lost. The domestic, slightly absurd image sits against a genuinely sad feeling. Dylan plays it straight, as a slow ballad, which makes the oddness of the conceit all the more touching.
day-in-day-out: The singer describes a love that keeps hitting him with the same force every single day, as if it were brand new each time. It is an energetic, driving song, its rhythm suggesting a pulse that will not slow down. Dylan's version moves along at a steady, swinging clip, a lively opening to the album's final disc.
i-couldnt-sleep-a-wink-last-night: The singer has had a falling-out with someone he loves and spent a sleepless night worrying, wanting only to make up. It is a tender, slightly anxious song, more sweet than sad, and it resolves with the hope of reconciliation. Dylan sings it softly and earnestly, the band giving it a gentle sway that suits a song about a restless night.
sentimental-journey: The song is about heading home after a long time away, with the train journey itself becoming a way to recover old memories. It caught the mood of the end of the Second World War, when many were making exactly that trip. Dylan gives it an easy, rolling rhythm and a warm, nostalgic tone, as if he were looking out of a train window himself.
somewhere-along-the-way: The singer looks back over a shared life and finds that the love slipped away at a moment he cannot pin down, somewhere between then and now. The song is regretful and searching, more puzzled than angry. Dylan sings it slowly, with a gentle, wistful arrangement that suits its sense of something lost without anyone quite noticing.
when-the-world-was-young: A sophisticated figure who seems to have everything admits he misses the simple pleasures and first loves of his younger years. The song sets the glamour of a grown-up life against memories of a more innocent time, and the memories win. Dylan's slow, rueful reading turns it into a portrait of an old man counting what he gave up.
these-foolish-things: The song is built from a list of tiny, ordinary things that bring a lost love back to mind, each one trivial on its own and painful in sum. It is affectionate and bittersweet rather than despairing. Dylan takes it gently, letting the band play a soft, swaying accompaniment while his voice lingers over the memories.
you-go-to-my-head: The singer describes being so taken with someone that it feels like drinking too much, a pleasant dizziness he cannot shake off. The song is sensual and a little woozy, full of images of intoxication. Dylan's version is slow and smoky, with the band laying down a hushed backdrop that suits its late-night, slightly tipsy mood.
stardust: A lonely singer looks up at the evening sky and drifts back to a romance that is long over. The song moves from a reflective, half-spoken opening into its famous soaring melody, where the memory of the affair becomes something to treasure in its own right. Its mood is wistful rather than bitter, more about the beauty of remembering than the pain of losing. Dylan takes it slowly and plainly, letting the tune carry the feeling, with a small band behind him.
its-funny-to-everyone-but-me: A jilted lover talks about being left behind while the people around him treat his heartbreak as a joke. The song turns on that gap between how his sorrow looks from outside and how it feels to him, mixing a little self-mockery into its sadness. It stays small and confiding, a single complaint told quietly rather than a grand lament. Dylan sings it as an unhurried late-night ballad, close and resigned.
why-was-i-born: A person in love with someone who does not love them back wonders aloud why they were ever born, if it was only to want what they cannot have. The song is built as a chain of plain, aching questions that never receive an answer. Its tone is torch-song despair softened by tenderness. As the final track of Triplicate, Dylan's slow, worn reading turns it into a quiet farewell to the whole songbook project.
ive-made-up-my-mind-to-give-myself-to-yo: A man who has lived a long, restless life speaks to the woman he loves and tells her he has finally settled his mind on giving himself to her. The song unfolds patiently, each verse returning to the same quiet resolution, as he looks back over his wandering and finds it led here. Its tone is tender and unhurried, with no irony at all. The arrangement is soft and lilting, close to a lullaby.
black-rider: The singer addresses a mysterious black rider who has been following him, a figure who reads as death, temptation or a darker side of himself. He warns the rider off, mixing defiance with weariness and the odd flash of dry humour. The song moves slowly and quietly, never raising its voice, which makes it all the more menacing. Its sound is hushed and bare, with gentle guitar and soft accompaniment around Dylan's close, low vocal.
mother-of-muses: Like an ancient poet, the singer opens by calling on the goddess who mothers the muses, asking her to help him sing. He then pays tribute to generals who cleared the way in the Second World War and to figures such as Elvis Presley and Martin Luther King, before turning to his own love for one of the muses and to his sense of age. The tone is solemn, grateful and personal. The music is slow and stately, almost a hymn.
the-mighty-quinn-quinn-the-eskimo: The song describes a gloomy, idle crowd waiting for something to happen, and a strange figure called Quinn the Eskimo whose arrival will change everything. Its verses sketch odd, comic scenes of boredom and frustration, and its big singalong chorus celebrates the coming of the hero. It is playful and nonsensical rather than serious, a party song with a hint of a parable. The Isle of Wight performance with the Band is loose, rough and good-humoured.
minstrel-boy: The song is about a wandering musician who has travelled a long way and grown tired, still on the move with no one to ease his load. It asks, again and again in its chorus, who will offer him some kindness for his trouble. The tone is affectionate and a little mournful, a portrait of the performer as a lonely drifter. The live Isle of Wight recording leans on the Band's harmony voices, giving it a ragged, gospel-tinged warmth.
